episodes.text: At age ten, Jim lost both parents within a year and was sent by Virginia relatives to live with his grandparents in Nebraska.

Jim traveled by train from Virginia to Nebraska in the care of Jake Marpole; on the journey a conductor mentioned a Bohemian immigrant girl in the car ahead who could only say 'We go Black Hawk, Nebraska' — Jim's first indirect encounter with Ántonia.
Jim married Genevieve Whitney, an advantageous match that advanced his career; she later lived independently and kept her own fortune.
Jim renewed his friendship with Ántonia after long years and made time for her within his busy professional life.
Jim completed a written manuscript about Ántonia and delivered it to his unnamed friend, titling it 'My Ántonia.'
Jim arrived by wagon at his grandfather's Nebraska farm before daybreak after a twenty-mile night drive with Otto Fuchs.
Jim's grandmother bathed and fed him on his first morning at the farm, remarking on how much he looked like his father.
Jim first saw the Shimerda immigrant family huddled on the Black Hawk platform with bundles and boxes; they were taken off separately by wagon.
Otto Fuchs told Jim about a pony named Dude bought for him at a sale; Otto had been riding him to test his temperament and declared him a perfect gentleman.

Jim went with his grandmother to dig potatoes in the garden, which was a quarter-mile from the farmhouse; grandmother pointed out her rattlesnake cane and warned Jim never to go there without a weapon.
Jim sat alone in the garden while grandmother walked back, experiencing a feeling of complete happiness and dissolving into the prairie landscape.
On Sunday, Jim and his grandparents drove with Otto Fuchs to bring provisions to the Shimerdas, who had come to live on a wild place with no garden, chicken-house, or much broken land.
Jim first met Ántonia face-to-face at her family's dugout homestead; she ran out to greet the Burdens, took Jim's hand, and they raced to Squaw Creek together.
Sitting in the tall red grass, Ántonia eagerly learned a score of English words from Jim — sky, blue, eyes — and tried to give him her silver ring, which he refused.
Jim met Mr. Shimerda for the first time; the old man bent over grandmother's hand and then looked long and searchingly into Jim's face.
Mr. Shimerda pleaded with grandmother to teach Ántonia English, showing her a bilingual alphabet book and saying 'Te-e-ach, te-e-ach my Ántonia!'
Jim got his pony Dude and began riding to the post-office twice a week, running errands for his grandfather's farm.
Ántonia came nearly every day to the Burden farm for reading lessons with Jim; together they explored the prairie, raided the watermelon patch, and she helped grandmother in the kitchen.
Mr. Shimerda found the two Russian settlers Pavel and Peter near the dog-town and began visiting them nearly every evening, sometimes bringing Ántonia.
Jim and Ántonia rode together to visit Peter at the Russian settlers' log house.
Jim and Ántonia visited Peter at the Russian settlers' house; Peter served watermelons and played harmonica for them, and told them he left Russia because of a 'great trouble.'

During a reading lesson on the prairie bank, Ántonia caught a dying green insect and sheltered it in her hair; she told Jim about Old Hata, a beggar woman from her village who sang to children — Ántonia had tears in her eyes.
Jim and Ántonia encountered Mr. Shimerda dragging himself slowly across the upland with a gun; Ántonia told Jim her father was sick all the time and did not look good.
Mr. Shimerda promised to give Jim his fine Bohemian gun when Jim grew up — a gun that had belonged to a great rich man who gave it to Shimerda for playing at his wedding.
Jim and Ántonia visited Russian Peter digging potatoes, then explored the prairie-dog-town with a borrowed spade.
Jim encountered a giant rattlesnake at the dog-town and killed it with the spade, striking it across the neck as it coiled to spring.
Ántonia praised Jim lavishly as brave after the snake-kill; her admiration reshaped how Jim felt about himself in that moment.
Jim and Ántonia dragged the dead rattlesnake home; Otto Fuchs examined it and confirmed it was the biggest rattler ever killed in those parts.
Jim later recognized that the snake encounter was a lucky mock-adventure — the snake was old and slow, the spade was borrowed by chance, and Ántonia's admiration amplified his courage.
Peter told Mr. Shimerda he could not meet a note due November 1 and had to pay an exorbitant bonus on renewal, giving mortgages on his pigs, horses, and milk cow to Wick Cutter.
Pavel strained himself lifting timbers for a new barn and suffered a massive lung hemorrhage, collapsing among the shavings; workmen hauled him home to bed very ill.
Jim persuaded grandmother to let him accompany Mr. Shimerda, Ántonia, and Peter to visit the dying Pavel; grandmother sent along sandwiches and doughnuts.

Jim and Ántonia sat up through the night at Pavel's bedside; Pavel coughed blood, raged deliriously about wolves, and dictated a long confession to Mr. Shimerda while Ántonia held Jim's hand under the table.

On the way home Ántonia told Jim the story Pavel had confessed: as young groomsmen in Russia, Pavel and Peter's wedding party was overtaken by hundreds of wolves; sledge after sledge was lost until only the groom's sledge remained.
Pavel died a few days after his confession and was buried in the Norwegian graveyard.
Peter sold off everything at auction and left for a railway construction camp to work as cook; the Black Hawk moneylender bought in his sale notes at fifty cents on the dollar.
Before leaving, Peter sat alone in his stripped house and ate all the melons he had saved for winter, surrounded by rinds when Mr. Shimerda and Krajiek came to take him to the train.
The wedding-party wolf story became a secret shared only between Jim and Ántonia; they guarded it jealously and it lingered in Jim's night imagination — sledges, horses, prairie.
First snowfall came early in December; Jim noticed the faint Indian ring on the hill slope showing clearly under a light cover of snow.

Jim drove Ántonia and Yulka in a homemade sleigh to Russian Peter's empty house and back; caught in the east wind on the return, he came down with quinsy and was confined indoors for nearly two weeks.
Confined by quinsy, Jim read 'The Swiss Family Robinson' aloud to grandmother each afternoon and marveled at her cheerful efficiency keeping the household warm and fed in bitter winter.

Otto sang cowboy songs on Saturday nights and led church singing at the sod schoolhouse; Jim vividly recalls the two men on the bench — tired shoulders, slicked hair — as examples of faithful, hard-working men who never got on.

Otto told the story of being asked to escort a woman on the boat to America who gave birth to triplets mid-ocean, making him an object of absurd suspicion — grandmother laughed until she wiped her eyes.
Weeks after the sleigh-ride, Fuchs reported Mr. Shimerda hunting in a homemade rabbit-skin cap and collar; the Shimerdas had only one overcoat to share and were living on what scraps they could find.
Grandmother and Jake drove to the Shimerdas with a hamper of food; they found the family in dire condition — rotten frozen potatoes, a nearly empty flour barrel, no coffee, feet wrapped in rags.
Mrs. Shimerda wept bitterly on the floor; Ántonia came reluctantly to help unpack the hamper, looking crushed — Jim had never seen her like that before.
Mr. Shimerda showed grandmother the hole in the cave wall where Yulka and Ántonia slept on straw; Ántonia insisted she liked it, warm as a badger hole.

Mr. Shimerda, speaking through Ántonia, explained to grandmother that they were not beggars — he had earned good wages in Bohemia, left with over a thousand dollars, but losses on exchange in New York and Krajiek's prices had nearly wiped them out.
Mrs. Shimerda gave grandmother a ceremonial gift of dried mushrooms from a cloth bag — grandmother burned them not knowing what they were; Jim tasted one and never forgot the strange earthy flavor.
A blizzard starting December 21 trapped everyone at the farm and prevented Jake from getting to town for Christmas shopping.

Jim and grandmother made a homemade picture book from cloth and magazine lithographs for Yulka and Ántonia; Jake cut a Christmas tree; Otto produced Austrian paper Christmas figures sent by his mother — the household had a country Christmas.
On Christmas morning grandfather read from Matthew and prayed for the destitute; his prayers gave the household its clearest window into his inner views.

Mr. Shimerda came Christmas afternoon to thank the Burdens; he sat by the stove in deep grateful peace, visibly moved by the order and comfort of the house, then knelt and crossed himself before the lit Christmas tree.
When Mr. Shimerda left, he bent over grandmother's hand and said 'Good woman!' — then made the sign of the cross over Jim.
Ántonia told Jim her father never wanted to come to America — his wife drove the emigration for Ambrosch's sake; Mr. Shimerda wept leaving behind the musician friends he loved.
Mrs. Shimerda visited the Burden house and left with a borrowed iron pot; Jim was furious and found it hard not to be cool toward Ántonia for her mother's grasping.
Jim reflected harshly that Mrs. Shimerda was conceited and boastful even in misfortune; grandmother gently reminded him that poverty brings out grasping in people.
A massive blizzard hit on Jim's eleventh birthday, January 20th — the worst storm in grandfather's ten years in Nebraska; Jake and Otto spent two days shoveling paths to the barn and hen-house.
On the morning of January 22nd, grandfather announced that Mr. Shimerda had been found dead — Ambrosch had come in the night and Otto and Jake went back with him.

Otto reported that Mr. Shimerda had shaved, washed, put on clean clothes, kissed Ántonia and Yulka, then took his gun to the barn and shot himself — he lay down on the bunk near the ox stalls where he always slept.
Jake noticed Krajiek's axe under the manger and briefly suspected murder, but Otto and grandfather concluded the wound was self-inflicted from inside outward.
Otto rode out alone through the blizzard on grandfather's best grey gelding to fetch the priest and coroner from Black Hawk.
Grandfather and grandmother rode to the Shimerdas' on the big black horses; Jim was left alone in the house for the first time.
While alone in the house after Mr. Shimerda's death, Jim sat quietly imagining the old man's spirit resting in the Burden kitchen — at peace before the long journey home to Bohemia.

Jake reported back that Mr. Shimerda's frozen body lay in the barn with a lantern over his head; the family and Marek took turns going down to pray beside him; Ambrosch was desperate to get a priest for fear his father's soul was in Purgatory.
Otto returned from Black Hawk with the news that the coroner was coming but the missionary priest was a hundred miles away; the grey gelding was permanently broken by the trip.
Otto brought Anton Jelinek — a young Bohemian homesteader near Black Hawk — to help; Jelinek broke a road to the Shimerdas' with the black farm-horses, and Otto set to work making the coffin.

At dinner Jelinek told of serving an old priest during the Prussian war, carrying the Sacrament among dying cholera soldiers — convinced they were both preserved from sickness by the holy vessels; grandfather respected his frank faith.
Otto Fuchs built Mr. Shimerda's coffin in the Burden kitchen from grandfather's planks, planning carefully before he started — he whistled and sang German hymns at his work.

Neighbours rode over — the postmaster Mr. Bushy, the Widow Steavens's brother, and a German neighbour — gathering to discuss where Mr. Shimerda could be buried; Norwegian church refused him as a suicide.
Grandfather brought the coroner — a one-armed Civil War veteran — back to the farm; the coroner said but for grandfather he might have sworn a warrant against Krajiek.

Mrs. Shimerda insisted on burying Mr. Shimerda at the southwest corner stake of their own land, where two roads would one day cross; grandfather warned she was mistaken if she thought people would ride over the old man's grave.
Jelinek and Ambrosch spent all day Friday chopping the frozen grave with old axes; on Saturday morning Jake and Jelinek rode ahead to cut the body free from the frozen pool of blood.
At the Shimerda house Ántonia ran out of her dark corner and threw her arms around Jim, sobbing about her lovely papa — Jim felt her heart breaking as she clung to him.

Mr. Shimerda lay four days in the barn; on the fifth day neighbours came on horseback and in wagon for the burial; Jim slipped out to view the coffin — Shimerda lay on his side, draped in black shawl, head in white muslin, one shapely hand visible.
At the burial, Yulka refused to touch the coffin in fright; grandmother intervened to protect her from Mrs. Shimerda's insistence; Ántonia held Yulka close.

Grandfather gave a graveside prayer over Mr. Shimerda that Jim still remembers — non-judgmental, asking God's forgiveness for any neighbor who had been remiss to the stranger, and commending Shimerda to God's judgment and mercy.
Otto led the mourners in 'Jesus, Lover of My Soul' at the graveside; Jim still remembers it whenever he hears the hymn.
In later years the roads curved around Shimerda's grave — as grandfather predicted — and the spot became the most dear to Jim in all that country.

Spring came after the hard winter; the Shimerdas were in their new log house by March, built with neighbours' help, with a new windmill on credit and livestock; Mrs. Shimerda bought a milk cow from grandfather for ten dollars down and fifteen after harvest.

In April Jim visited the Shimerdas; Ántonia was now working the fields with Ambrosch, ploughing sod all day — she refused to go to school, saying she could work like a man and needed to help make the land a good farm.

After supper at the Shimerdas' in April, Jim noticed Ántonia ate noisily, yawned, and stretched like a tired field hand — grandmother's prediction ('heavy field work'll spoil that girl') seemed to have come true.

Jake and Jim rode to the Shimerdas' to retrieve a borrowed horse-collar; Ambrosch returned it ruined — trampled and rat-gnawed — and when Jake confronted him, Ambrosch kicked at Jake, and Jake knocked him down with a blow to the head.
Ántonia and Mrs. Shimerda ran screaming through the pond to defend Ambrosch; Ántonia declared she would never be friends with Jake and Jim again.
Grandfather advised Jake to go to a justice of the peace and pay a fine proactively; Jake went to town Monday and paid with a ten-dollar bill grandfather gave him, also selling a pig.
Mrs. Shimerda and Ambrosch drove past the Burden farm looking neither left nor right on Monday; grandfather had expected her to follow up.
For weeks afterward Ántonia jeered at Jake from the road: 'Jake-y, Jake-y, sell the pig and pay the slap!' — a cold phase opened between Jim and the Shimerdas.
Ambrosch sold his oxen to a German settler and bought horses with grandfather's guidance; put Marek to hard work but could never teach him to cultivate corn properly.

While Ambrosch and Marek were away at Mr. Bushy's, Ántonia and Mrs. Shimerda ran the farm alone; one of the new horses got colic and Ántonia rode bareback to the Burdens to fetch grandfather in the night.

When Ambrosch returned from Mr. Bushy's he had given Marek's wages to the priest at Black Hawk for Masses for their father's soul; grandmother thought Ántonia needed shoes more, but grandfather said it showed Ambrosch believed what he professed.
Grandfather rode to the Shimerdas' and made peace — engaged Ambrosch and Ántonia for the harvest — then surprised Mrs. Shimerda by forgiving the remaining fifteen dollars on the cow.
Mrs. Shimerda knelt and kissed grandfather's hand in gratitude for forgiving the cow debt; grandfather was more embarrassed than Jim had ever seen him.
The next Sunday Mrs. Shimerda came over with a pair of handknit socks for Jake as a peace offering; Jake cheerfully gave her the last word.

In July, during harvest season, Ántonia came to work in the Burden kitchen and garden; she and Jim went to the garden each morning, and she threw off her sunbonnet and sang about preferring outdoor work.
One night during harvest Ántonia and Jim climbed onto the chicken-house roof to watch an electric storm; grandmother called them in.
Grandfather decided to move the family to Black Hawk when Jim was thirteen, renting the homestead to the Widow Steavens and buying Preacher White's house at the north end of town.
Jake and Otto helped move the Burdens into Black Hawk, then left without warning on the westbound train — Jim never saw them again.

Months after they left, a card arrived saying Jake had mountain fever but both were working the Yankee Girl Mine in Colorado; Jim wrote but the letter came back unclaimed and they were never heard from again.
Grandmother arranged for Ántonia to stop farm-labor and come work with the neighboring Harling family in Black Hawk.
Mrs. Harling and Frances drove out to the Shimerda homestead to meet Ántonia and negotiated her wages with Ambrosch — three dollars a week plus shoes, with fifty dollars a year for Ántonia's own use.
Ántonia arrived in Black Hawk on Saturday, running into the Burden kitchen as she used to; grandmother kissed her and charged her to do right.
Lena Lingard arrived at the Harling house dressed as a town girl and announced she had come to Black Hawk to work as a dressmaker's apprentice for Mrs. Thomas.
Crazy Mary chased Lena across the prairie and into the Shimerdas' house, threatening her with a corn-knife; Ántonia sent Mary away with an apronful of tomatoes.
In Black Hawk, Jim often walked with Lena when she was on errands for Mrs. Thomas, and heard about hotel entertainments through her and Tiny Soderball.
Ántonia told the Harling household the story of a suicidal tramp who jumped head-first into a threshing machine at the Iverson farm during harvest.
Jim and the Harlings skated on the river through January and February, making bonfires on the frozen sand of the big island.
Blind d'Arnault, a Negro pianist, came to perform at the Black Hawk Opera House and stayed at the Boys' Home Hotel; Mrs. Harling arranged for Ántonia to go hear him.
Jim slipped into the Boys' Home Hotel parlour and watched traveling men sing Negro melodies with Blind d'Arnault at the piano.
Ántonia, Lena, Tiny Soderball, and Mary Dusak were discovered waltzing in the hotel dining-room while d'Arnault played — Kirkpatrick burst in and tried to bring them in to dance with the men.
Jim walked Ántonia home from the d'Arnault hotel dance; they lingered a long while at the Harlings' gate whispering in the cold, too excited to go in.
Jim helped Mrs. Harling and Tony break ground, plant the garden, and tend the orchard in spring — the happiest weeks of that winter's end.
A dancing pavilion arrived in Black Hawk in June — Italian traveling teachers the Vannis set up a tent near the Danish laundry; Jim attended every Saturday night dance without fail.

Sylvester Lovett, cashier at his father's bank, became infatuated with Lena Lingard at the Vanni dances — drove miles to visit her, grew distracted at work — then ran off with a widow who owned a half-section to escape his predicament; Jim felt contempt for him.
Ántonia became the best dancer at the Vanni tent and was 'discovered' socially — throngs of boys came to the back door of the Harlings seeking dances with her; a crisis with Mr. Harling was building.
Harry Paine — about to be married on Monday — tried to kiss Ántonia on the Harlings' back porch after the dance; she slapped him free and he vaulted over the fence; Mr. Harling witnessed the scene.
Mr. Harling gave Ántonia an ultimatum: stop going to the dances or leave; she refused to stop dancing and chose to leave the Harling household.
Ántonia left the Harlings and went to work for the Cutters — Mrs. Harling warned it would be her ruin; the kitchen crockery trembled when Mrs. Harling walked out.
After moving to the Cutters', Ántonia seemed to care only about picnics, parties, and fine clothes — copying the dress of well-off Black Hawk ladies under Lena's direction.

Jim, as a senior, began slipping out his bedroom window on Saturday nights to attend the Firemen's Hall dances — deceiving his grandparents, who disapproved; the dances were the one thing he looked forward to all week.
Anton Jelinek had rented his homestead, moved to Black Hawk, and opened a saloon catering to Bohemian and German farmers — he asked Jim to stop visiting out of respect for grandfather.
Jim walked Ántonia home from the Cutters' one night and told her he must kiss her; she scolded him, warned him about Lena, and urged him to go away to school and make something of himself.
Grandmother discovered Jim had been sneaking out to the Firemen's Hall dances and wept; Jim promised to stop, and kept his word — spending the spring evenings reading Latin at home.
Jim gave the commencement oration at the Black Hawk Opera House and impressed Mrs. Harling; afterward Ántonia, Lena, and Anna Hansen waited for him under the maples to praise him.

The day after commencement Jim moved upstairs and worked through trigonometry and Virgil all summer — Mrs. Harling championed his cause to grandfather when the grandparents had misgivings about his going to college alone.
Jim joined Ántonia, Lena, Tiny, and Anna Hansen for a picnic at the river — his one holiday that summer; he swam and they drove over the bridge calling cheerfully to each other.
Under the elder bushes at the river Jim found Ántonia alone and crying — the elderflower smell brought her father back; she told Jim the story of her father's marriage and her grandmother's house.
Jim joined Ántonia, Lena Lingard, Tiny Soderball, and Anna on a summer river picnic — they climbed the chalk bluffs, shared lunch, played games on the flat top, and watched the sun go down together.

Jim told the girls about Coronado and the Seven Golden Cities, recounting how he and Charley Harling believed the explorer had reached their very river — supported by a Spanish sword and stirrup found by a local farmer and displayed in the Harling office.

At sunset Jim and the girls witnessed a plough left standing on an upland farm silhouetted heroically against the sun's disk — a vision that burned itself into memory before disappearing as the sun dropped below the horizon.

Ántonia came to the Burdens troubled, reporting that Wick Cutter had placed his silver and valuables under her bed before leaving for Omaha and made her promise to sleep there alone — she feared he was 'up to some of his tricks.'
Grandmother arranged for Jim to sleep at the Cutters' house in Ántonia's place, so Ántonia could stay safe under the Burdens' roof; Jim agreed reluctantly for Tony's sake.

On the third night at the Cutters', Wick Cutter returned in the dark and attacked Jim in Ántonia's bed — choking him, beating him in the face — before Jim broke free, knocked Cutter to the floor, dove through the window screen, and ran home across Black Hawk in his nightshirt.

Jim was badly beaten — cut lip, blue swollen nose, eye swollen shut — and begged grandmother not to send for a doctor or let anyone see him; grandmother spent the morning nursing his bruises with arnica while he lay facing the wall, furious and humiliated.
Grandfather discovered at the depot that Cutter had come home on the night express, left again for Denver at six a.m. with a bandaged face and his left hand in a sling.
Ántonia and grandmother went to the Cutters' and found her room ransacked — clothes torn and trampled, Jim's garments destroyed; grandmother burned his clothes in the Cutters' kitchen range.

Mrs. Cutter arrived at her own house locked out, head trembling with rage; grandmother told her what had happened and kept her from seeing Ántonia; Mrs. Cutter revealed Cutter had tricked her onto a Kansas City express at Waymore Junction to get back to Black Hawk without her.
Jim entered the university at Lincoln and came immediately under the influence of Gaston Cleric, head of the Latin department — Cleric became his examiner and arranged his course.

Jim stayed in Lincoln for his first summer vacation working off a year's Greek; he and Cleric played tennis, read, and took long walks — Jim later looked back on that summer as one of the happiest of his life.

During a sophomore evening in March, reading the Georgics, Jim found Cleric's explanation of 'patria' as one's own rural neighborhood — not a nation — unlocking something deep in him about Nebraska and his own past.
Lena Lingard turned up unannounced at Jim's Lincoln room one evening — she had opened a dressmaking shop in the Raleigh Block on O Street and had been in Lincoln all winter without telling him.
Lena told Jim that Ántonia was now housekeeper at Mrs. Gardener's hotel, had reconciled with the Harlings, and was engaged to Larry Donovan — Jim said he didn't like Larry and never would.
After Lena left Jim's room, the connection between country girls like her and the poetry of Virgil struck Jim as an inestimable revelation — the two worlds fused in his mind for the first time.

That spring Jim went with Lena to see Joseph Jefferson in 'Rip Van Winkle,' a war play called 'Shenandoah,' 'Robin Hood,' and finally to 'Camille' — Lena paid her own way each time, insisting she was in business now.
Jim and Lena saw 'Camille' together — the play wrecked them both; Lena cowered and covered her face when Armand flung money at Marguerite, and Jim wept unrestrainedly in the final scene.

After Camille, Jim walked Lena home under Mrs. Harling's silk umbrella and then tramped alone through the spring rain mourning Marguerite Gauthier as if she had died yesterday — the spirit of 1840 reaching him across years and languages.

Jim became a regular visitor at Lena's shop — Sunday breakfasts in her bay-window alcove with her water-spaniel Prince; afternoon walks downtown; evenings spent watching her drape satin on a wire figure.

Jim fell into a drift of ease in Lincoln — playing with Lena and Prince, playing with Ordinsky, going buggy-riding with old Colonel Raleigh; he admitted Lena had broken up his serious mood and he wasn't interested in his classes.

Ordinsky the Polish violin teacher confronted Jim with prickly suspicion about his visits to Lena; Jim answered him plainly and they reached an understanding — afterward Ordinsky was friendly and acted as if some deep chivalric bond existed between them.
Cleric was offered and accepted an instructorship at Harvard before June; he urged Jim to follow him East in the fall.
Cleric wrote grandfather asking to take Jim East; grandfather agreed Jim could go if he wished.
Jim visited Lena the night after the letter came and told her he was leaving Lincoln for Harvard.
Lena sent Jim away with a renunciatory kiss — sweet and accepting, never trying to hold him back.
Jim closed his Lincoln chapter: visited his grandparents for a few weeks, then visited Virginia relatives, then joined Cleric in Boston at age nineteen.
Two years after leaving Lincoln, Jim completed his academic course at Harvard and returned home to Black Hawk for summer before law school.
Frances Harling told Jim that Ántonia had gone to marry Larry Donovan, was deserted, had a baby, and had come home to the farm — never married, now Ambrosch's drudge.
Tiny Soderball quietly went West to Seattle and opened a sailors' lodging-house in a waterfront building offered by a promoter from the Boys' Home Hotel.
Frances Harling was married by the time Jim returned, and she and her husband managed the Harling business interests in Black Hawk.
Tiny Soderball sold her Seattle lodging-house, joined a carpenter and his wife, and trekked to Alaska — through Skaguay, over the Chilkoot Pass, and down the Yukon in flatboats to Circle City.
Tiny and her party reached Circle City the day Siwash Indians reported a gold strike on Klondike Creek; they joined the last steamer up the Yukon before freeze-up and helped found Dawson City.
Tiny cooked for miners in a tent in Dawson; a miners' gift of a building lot and a carpenter's labor gave her a log hotel where she fed up to 150 men a day and sold bread for gold.
A Swedish miner (Johnson) with frozen, amputated feet deeded Tiny his Hunker Creek claim before dying; Tiny sold the hotel, invested half her money in Dawson lots, and developed the claim herself.
After nearly ten years in the Klondike, Tiny returned to San Francisco with a considerable fortune.
Jim met Tiny in Salt Lake City in 1908 — thin, hard-faced, well-dressed; she mentioned losing three toes to frostbite on Hunker Creek.
Tiny had persuaded Lena to move her dressmaking business from Lincoln to San Francisco, saying 'Lincoln was never any place for her.'

Jim saw Ántonia's baby's portrait at the Black Hawk photographer's — in a large gilt frame — and felt he must go see Ántonia again; he could forgive her everything but throwing herself away on Larry Donovan.
Mrs. Harling directed Jim to visit the Widow Steavens on his grandfather's farm for the full story of Ántonia's failed marriage.
Jim rode out to his grandfather's old place in August to visit the Widow Steavens — she agreed to tell him everything about Ántonia after supper.
Mrs. Steavens told Jim that before her departure Ántonia came daily to the Steavens house all summer to sew her trousseau on their machine, singing Bohemian songs and working with great energy.
Ambrosch gave Ántonia a set of plated silver in a purple velvet box and three hundred dollars — her collected wages — when she left for Denver; Mrs. Steavens praised him for it.
Ántonia departed for Denver in March in mud and rain, waving goodbye to the Steavens house and whispering 'Goodbye, dear house.'
Donovan delayed the marriage in Denver, was already fired and blacklisted for knocking down fares; he lived off Ántonia's money until it ran out, then vanished — likely fled to Mexico.

Mrs. Steavens found Ántonia back at the Shimerda farm, standing over wash-tubs in the middle of the week — the bridal underclothes swinging on the line; Ántonia told her quietly she was not married and ought to be.
Marek Shimerda had grown violent and been sent away to an institution sometime before Ántonia's return.

All that spring and summer after her return, Ántonia ploughed corn and did the work of a man on the farm — quiet, steady, never wearing her pretty dresses, never going anywhere; she developed bad toothache and wouldn't go to Black Hawk for a dentist.
Ántonia herded Ambrosch's cattle through the fall — sitting on grassy banks, sunning herself, reflecting on old times with Jim and her father — growing visibly heavier into winter.
In December Ántonia drove her cattle home through a snowstorm and gave birth alone that night in her room, without calling for help or making a sound.
Mrs. Steavens and her brother William rushed over and assisted at the birth; Ambrosch refused to look at the baby and said to put it in the rain-barrel — Mrs. Steavens cowed him by invoking the law.
Gaston Cleric died of pneumonia the winter before Jim's reunion with Ántonia.
Jim walked to the Shimerdas' the next afternoon; he and Ántonia met silently in the field and sat together by Mr. Shimerda's grave to talk.
Jim told Ántonia everything: his decision to study law and enter a New York law office, and Cleric's death — she listened and asked about his friends and his hopes.
At parting Jim held Ántonia's hands against his heart in the darkening field, meaning to carry her face with him — the closest, realest face at the bottom of his memory.
Jim kept his promise to return but twenty years passed before he did — life intervened, and he feared finding Ántonia aged and broken.
Jim learned that soon after their last meeting Ántonia married a young Bohemian named Cuzak, a cousin of Anton Jelinek; they were poor and had a large family.
In San Francisco Jim saw Lena and Tiny together — Tiny audits Lena's accounts and invests her money; Lena makes sure Tiny doesn't grow miserly.
Lena urged Jim to visit Ántonia, saying Cuzak isn't a hustler but a rough man would never have suited Tony, and that she has ten or eleven children by now.
Jim broke his journey at Hastings, Nebraska, hired an open buggy, and drove to the Cuzak farm, finding two boys mourning a dead dog in a plum thicket beside the road.
Jim arrived at the Cuzak farm: a wide farmhouse with red barn and ash grove; he was met by a light-footed curly-headed boy (Leo, twelve, born on Easter) and two girls washing dishes.
Ántonia came in, recognized Jim with widening eyes after a moment, and rushed to gather all her children to meet him — 'battered but not diminished,' in the full vigour of her personality.

Ántonia showed Jim her fruit cave — three barrels of dill pickles, chopped pickles, and pickled watermelon rind, and shelves of preserved cherries, strawberries, and crabapples; the children ran up the cellar stairs into the sunlight in a 'veritable explosion of life.'

Ántonia walked Jim through her apple orchard — every tree planted by hand, watered by her after long field days; Cuzak had been a city man who got discouraged, but she cared for the trees like children.
Jan Cuzak told his mother about the dead dog in Bohemian, weeping; she soothed him and whispered a promise that made him smile — he slipped off to tell Nina the secret.
Jim visited the Cuzak farm; Ántonia told him how glad she was to have gone to town and learned housekeeping at the Harlings' — she credits that education for raising her children well.
Jim helped the Cuzak boys drive cows home at sunset and told them he had once been in love with their mother.
After supper Leo played Mr. Shimerda's old violin (too big for him but self-taught) and little Nina danced barefoot on the parlour floor unnoticed.
Ántonia brought out a box of family photographs — including her and Cuzak in wedding clothes, Ambrosch and his fat bossy wife, and the three Bohemian Marys with their large families.
Ántonia showed the family a photograph of Lena Lingard from San Francisco — Lena had not been home to Nebraska for six years.
Jim slept in the haymow with Leo and Ambrosch Cuzak; lying awake by the open window he contemplated Ántonia as a rich mine of life, a founder of early races.
The Cuzak children found an old tintype of Jim with Jake Marpole and Otto Fuchs taken on the first Fourth of July in Nebraska — Ántonia expressed shame for her quarrel with Jake.

Rudolph Cuzak told the family at supper the story of the Cutter murder-suicide: Wick Cutter shot Mrs. Cutter through the heart while she napped, then shot himself at six o'clock, surviving long enough to declare witnesses present that he had outlived his wife.
Cuzak returned from a holiday in Wilber with Rudolph; they had attended dances and seen the Bohemian crowd.
Jim and Cuzak smoked in the orchard after supper; Cuzak told Jim his life story — Vienna furrier, New York strike scab, Florida freeze, then Nebraska via Jelinek and Ántonia.
Jim said goodbye to Ántonia and the children the morning after Cuzak returned, drove back to Hastings and took the train to Black Hawk.
Jim's day in Black Hawk was disappointing — most old friends dead or gone, the Harlings' yard full of strangers, the mountain ash cut down.
Jim spent the morning with Anton Jelinek under a cottonwood behind his saloon, then discussed the Cutter murder case with an old lawyer.

Walking north of Black Hawk into rough unploughed pastures, Jim stumbled upon a half-mile of the original road to his grandfather's farm — the only surviving stretch; he sat down and meditated on the road of Destiny that had brought him and Ántonia together and would bring them together again.

communication.label: Communication style
communication.line: How they like to be spoken to.

life.label: Life
life.line: Born in Virginia, parents died at ten; raised by grandparents on a Nebraska farm, moved to Black Hawk at thirteen; chafed against the town's smallness, gave his commencement speech, escaped to university; beaten and shamed by Cutter; now over forty, based in New York, childless, a railway lawyer — his emotional country is Nebraska, not Manhattan

life/black-hawk-social.label: Black Hawk social world
life/black-hawk-social.line: The social fabric of Jim's Black Hawk years — country hired girls electrified the town while merchant-class daughters sat indoors calling themselves refined; the Vanni tent and Firemen's Hall dances were the heartbeat of the summer; Blind d'Arnault's concert was a richer evening than anything the town had known; Jim sneaked out his window every Saturday until grandmother wept and he gave his word to stop

life/black-hawk-years.label: Black Hawk years
life/black-hawk-years.line: Moved to Black Hawk at thirteen — the winters bleak and cold, Jim chafed against the town's repressive smallness as a senior, sneaked out to dances, then gave his commencement speech and left for university

life/nebraska-farm.label: Nebraska farm years
life/nebraska-farm.line: The Burden homestead — only wooden house for miles, rented to the Widow Steavens when the family moved to town; Mr. Shimerda's crossroads grave the most beloved spot in all that country, never passed without emotion

life/university-lincoln.label: University years in Lincoln
life/university-lincoln.line: Jim's freshman and sophomore years in Lincoln — intellectual awakening under Cleric, room near open country with Roman map and Pompeii photo, old Nebraska figures rising unbidden during every moment of mental excitement

money-style.label: Money style
money-style.line: How they handle money: discipline, risk, planning.

people.label: People
people.line: Jim's world of people: grandparents who raised him, Ántonia the heart of his Nebraska childhood, a distant wife, Jake and Otto who made the journey with him, the exploitative Krajiek, the grieving Shimerdas, the haunting Russian settlers Pavel and Peter, Anton Jelinek, and the hired-girl circle — Tiny Soderball, Lena Lingard, and others who grew up hard and went far

people/anton-jelinek.label: Anton Jelinek
people/anton-jelinek.line: Strapping young Bohemian neighbor who rode to help the Shimerdas in their grief — warm-hearted, frank, manly faith; broke the road to their homestead and Jim admired him immediately

people/antonia.label: Ántonia
people/antonia.line: Bohemian immigrant girl, the heart of Jim's Nebraska childhood — battered by hardship and Donovan's desertion but never diminished; the fire of life still burning at forty; married Cuzak, raised ten children, planted an orchard; rooted in the land — she would be miserable in a city; the closest, realest face at the bottom of Jim's memory; waving her apron at the windmill as he drove away

people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings.label: Ántonia at the Harlings
people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings.line: Ántonia's Black Hawk household chapter — warm fit with the Harlings, best dancer discovered at the Vanni tent, then crisis and departure to the Cutters against Mrs. Harling's dire warning

people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings/danci.label: Ántonia's dancing crisis and departure
people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings/danci.line: Best dancer at the Vanni tent — dancing obsession drew men to the back gate; Harry Paine's forced kiss was the flashpoint, Mr. Harling's ultimatum forced a choice, and Ántonia left for the Cutters against Mrs. Harling's warning that it would ruin her

people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings/harli.label: Ántonia's fit at the Harlings
people/antonia/antonia-at-harlings/harli.line: Placed at seventeen by grandmother — learned English fast, admired Charley, loved the children; wages fought over with Ambrosch, but Mrs. Harling kept her own allowance; basic harmony with the household, a place Jim couldn't imagine her leaving

people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family.label: Ántonia Cuzak's family
people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family.line: Ántonia married Cuzak and built a large, rooted Bohemian family on the Nebraska farm — the children proud of her, full of life; the first ten years hard but she carried them; the farm itself planted with her own hands; a joyful, tightly knit household speaking Bohemian at home

people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family/cuza.label: The Cuzak children
people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family/cuza.line: Ántonia's children — ten or eleven in all — are a joyful, proud, Bohemian-speaking brood: Anna (eldest, steady), Leo (wild, faun-faced, born Easter, best-loved, plays Shimerda's violin, sceptical as old Mrs. Shimerda), Rudolph (six-foot baritone), Nina (named for Nina Harling), Jan (bashful), Martha (born before marriage, now married with her own baby); all proud of their mother and looking to her for stories; Frances Harling a heroine in family legend

people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family/cuza.label: Cuzak farm life — orchard, cave, and struggle
people/antonia/antonia-cuzak-family/cuza.line: The farm near Hastings — wide house with red barn, ash grove, cattle-yards — was built up from nothing: first ten years a hard struggle, Cuzak often discouraged, Ántonia's strength carrying them through; she planted every orchard tree by hand and watered it after field days; the fruit cave a testament to her industry — pickles, preserves, cherries, crabapples; the place now paid for and worth five times the price

people/antonia/antonia-donovan-period.label: Ántonia — Donovan, desertion, and return
people/antonia/antonia-donovan-period.line: Ántonia was deserted by Larry Donovan before she even arrived in Denver — he had been fired and blacklisted, lived off her money, then vanished; she returned unmarried and pregnant, quiet and dignified, bore the child alone without a cry, and drudged on the farm for Ambrosch; Jim could forgive her anything except Donovan; she showed no shame for the baby and told Mrs. Steavens she was 'not married and ought to be'

people/antonia/antonia-growing-up.label: Ántonia growing up — labor and distance
people/antonia/antonia-growing-up.line: After her father's death Ántonia hardened fast: ploughing from sunup to sundown at fifteen, too proud of her strength, talking only of prices and endurance; she gave up school and the friendship with Jim cooled — she thought of him only as a little boy

people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond.label: Jim and Ántonia — shared memories and bond
people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond.line: The deepest bond in Jim's life — shared childhood dread and triumph (the snake, Pavel's dying vigil, the wolf-wedding secret), her father's grief carried hand-in-hand, and a declaration twenty years later that she is the closest realest face at the bottom of his memory; the old road back to his grandfather's farm is the road of Destiny for both — whatever they missed, they possess together the precious, incommunicable past

people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/bond-and.label: Jim and Ántonia — emotional bond and declaration
people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/bond-and.line: Jim's love for Ántonia runs the length of his life — fairest of them all, her voice went straight to his heart, he dedicated his commencement speech to her father; twenty years later she is a rich mine of life, the closest realest face at the bottom of his memory; she kept a newspaper photo of him; her grief for her father is a standing tenderness between them

people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/bond-and.label: Ántonia's father grief — a thread in the bond
people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/bond-and.line: Ántonia's grief for her father runs through the bond like a living thread — the elderflower smell still makes her cry, she told Jim her feet remember every path in her old country, and she counts her father more real than the living; Jim felt his presence at the deathbed and reassured her; grandmother called Ántonia his darling, left alone in a hard world

people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/shared-e.label: Jim and Ántonia — shared episodes and memories
people/antonia/jim-antonia-bond/shared-e.line: The foundational episodes Jim and Ántonia shared: killing the rattlesnake together (she later called him braver for it), sitting hand-in-hand through Pavel's dying wolf-confession, and keeping that horror as their private secret; Jim felt Mr. Shimerda's presence at the deathbed and later told Ántonia, which moved her deeply

people/antonia/shimerda-family.label: Shimerda family situation
people/antonia/shimerda-family.line: The Shimerdas — nearest Burden neighbors — arrived near-destitute (savings lost to Krajiek), survived near-starvation in a cave that first winter, built a log house by spring; grandfather's reconciliation closed the feud and he forgave the cow debt; Marek grew violent and was institutionalized; Ambrosch eventually married a fat bossy wife; Mrs. Shimerda proud and grasping throughout

people/antonia/shimerda-family/ambrosch.label: Ambrosch Shimerda
people/antonia/shimerda-family/ambrosch.line: Head of the Shimerda household after his father's death — controlling, devout, mean-handed; but gave Ántonia her three hundred dollars in wages and silver before her departure — one flash of decency amid habitual surly hardness

people/gaston-cleric.label: Gaston Cleric
people/gaston-cleric.line: Brilliant young Latin scholar, Jim's intellectual father at university — took an instructorship at Harvard and brought Jim East; died of pneumonia that winter; a permanent debt of gratitude and a standing loss

people/genevieve-burden.label: Genevieve Burden (wife)
people/genevieve-burden.line: Jim's wife; married him when he was obscure, advancing his career; lives her own life and keeps her own fortune — the marriage is cool and distant, her temperament irritates Jim

people/grandfather.label: Grandfather Burden
people/grandfather.line: Jim's grandfather; deliberate, dignified, a man of few words — white-bearded and imposing, inspired quiet awe in Jim from the start

people/grandmother.label: Grandmother Burden
people/grandmother.line: Jim's grandmother; tall, spare, energetic, fifty-five when he arrived — she raised him in Nebraska with warmth and anxious care, wept when he came and quickly turned brisk

people/harlings.label: The Harling family
people/harlings.line: Norwegian neighbors in Black Hawk — energetic Mrs. Harling championed Jim's university plans; Frances the shrewd clerk who rescued farmers from Cutter's clutches, now married managing the family interests; Ántonia credits the Harlings for teaching her to raise children well; Frances has come down as a heroine in the Cuzak family legend

people/jake-marpole.label: Jake Marpole
people/jake-marpole.line: Farm hand from Jim's Virginia home, traveled to Nebraska and left for Colorado prospecting after the Black Hawk move — never seen again, a standing loss Jim mourns

people/krajiek.label: Peter Krajiek
people/krajiek.line: Bohemian countryman who sold the Shimerdas their homestead at an inflated price, then overcharged them for a cookstove and worn-out horses — exploited them as their only interpreter; Jim regards him with contempt

people/lena-lingard.label: Lena Lingard
people/lena-lingard.line: Norwegian farm girl risen to leading San Francisco dressmaker via Lincoln — violet-eyed, warmly self-reliant, accountable to nobody; sent Jim away with a renunciatory kiss and never looked back; Tiny audits her accounts; hasn't been home to Nebraska for six years

people/lena-lingard/lena-lincoln.label: Lena Lingard — Lincoln years
people/lena-lingard/lena-lincoln.line: In Lincoln Lena opened her shop in the Raleigh Block, went to every play with Jim, and built her mother's house — three men fell for her that spring (Jim, Ordinsky the Polish violin teacher, and old Colonel Raleigh); Cleric confronted Jim and called her irresponsible; she was candid as Nature, habitually late, had a gift for knowing what people looked well in, and finally sent Jim away East with a renunciatory kiss

people/lena-lingard/lena-origins.label: Lena Lingard — prairie origins
people/lena-lingard/lena-origins.line: Grew up barefoot herding cattle in the Norwegian settlement, chased by Crazy Mary, talked about for making Ole Benson lose his senses — came to Black Hawk to sew and break free of farm life; has Lapp blood and owns it

people/mary-dusak.label: Mary Dusak
people/mary-dusak.line: Hired country girl in Black Hawk — handsome, bold, resourceful, and unscrupulous; beautiful chestnut hair and commanding dark eyes

people/mr-shimerda.label: Mr. Shimerda (Ántonia's father)
people/mr-shimerda.line: Ántonia's father — dignified, melancholy Bohemian weaver and fiddler who died by his own hand in January, homesick for Bohemia — his crossroads grave is the spot most dear to Jim in all that country, a standing grief; Ántonia talks to him still and counts him more real than the living; his violin lives on, played by Leo; Jim never forgot his sad, pitying smile

people/mr-shimerda/bohemia-life.label: Mr. Shimerda's life in Bohemia
people/mr-shimerda/bohemia-life.line: A weaver, fiddler, and educated man in Bohemia — played at weddings and dances, priests came to talk to him; forests, music, and friends he wept to leave; his wife drove the emigration for Ambrosch; the music died in Nebraska, never to return

people/mr-shimerda/death-and-grave.label: Mr. Shimerda — death and burial
people/mr-shimerda/death-and-grave.line: Shot himself in the barn in January — prepared carefully, dressed in clean clothes, kissed his daughters; buried at the crossroads of the Shimerda land (refused by the Norwegian graveyard); in later years the roads curved around the grave and tall red grass grew over it like a little island — the spot most dear to Jim in all that country, a grief that never passes; Jim believed homesickness killed him

people/mrs-shimerda.label: Mrs. Shimerda (Ántonia's mother)
people/mrs-shimerda.line: Ántonia's mother — shrewd, boastful, conceited, and grasping; she drove the family's emigration for Ambrosch's sake with no regard for her husband's grief; poverty sharpened rather than humbled her

people/otto-fuchs.label: Otto Fuchs
people/otto-fuchs.line: Grandfather's hired man who made the journey west with Jim — frontier character, faithful through sun and storm, left for the wild West after Black Hawk move and was never heard from again; a standing loss

people/pavel-peter.label: Pavel and Peter (Russian settlers)
people/pavel-peter.line: Two Russian settlers now gone — Pavel dead, having confessed he threw the bride and groom to the wolves to save the last sledge; Peter ruined by Wick Cutter's debt, sold everything, ate his winter melons alone in the stripped house, then vanished to a railway camp; their catastrophe left Jim haunted

people/tiny-soderball.label: Tiny Soderball
people/tiny-soderball.line: Brisk hired girl who gambled everything on the Klondike — endured the Chilkoot Pass, helped found Dawson City, inherited Johnson's gold claim, came home to San Francisco with a considerable fortune; the cost was three toes and the faculty of wonder; she audits Lena's accounts and persuaded Lena to move her shop to San Francisco

people/vannis.label: The Vannis (dancing teachers)
people/vannis.line: Italian traveling dancing-teachers who pitched their tent in Black Hawk in summer — Mrs. Vanni taught children, Mr. Vanni played harp; they transformed the empty summer evenings

people/wick-cutter.label: Wick Cutter
people/wick-cutter.line: Black Hawk's money-lender and sexual predator — merciless with debt, dissolute, hypocritically pious; tricked his wife onto a train to assault Ántonia's bed (finding Jim instead); in old age shot his wife through the heart while she slept and then himself, to prevent her relatives inheriting — his spite outlasted his life

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.line: Romantic and ardent — mythologizes place and the past, invests deeply in the West and its hard-worn people; acts first and reflects after; honest about his own self-myth but quick to shame; finds vitality in those who grew up hard rather than advantaged; despises small-town evasion and gossip

temperament/inner-life.label: Inner imaginative life
temperament/inner-life.line: Inhabits a rich interior world — mythologizes the past, invests places and people with deep personal meaning, guards cherished memories against disappointment, and surrenders completely to art; honest about the gap between experience and the story he makes of it

temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.label: Jim's mythologizing of Nebraska and its people
temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.line: Jim invests Nebraska, its landscapes and people, with mythic lasting meaning — the plough against the sun is 'picture writing,' the old road back to grandfather's farm is the road of Destiny; old Nebraska figures rise at every flash of mental excitement; he guards cherished memories against present disappointment, dreaded finding Ántonia broken and deferred the visit twenty years

temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.label: Nebraska as mythic homeland
temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.line: Jim experiences Nebraska as his mythic homeland — the plough against the sun was 'picture writing,' the sun-and-moon parting made him want to be a little boy again; at university old Nebraska figures rose vividly at every flash of excitement; Virgil's 'patria' reframed his Nebraska past as his country and source; the old road north of Black Hawk is the road of Destiny — he and Ántonia possess together the precious, incommunicable past

temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.label: Jim's protective investment in memory
temperament/inner-life/mythologizing-neb.line: Jim guards cherished memories against the risk of present disappointment — prefers the image to the encounter when the stakes are high; dreaded finding Ántonia aged and broken and deferred the visit twenty years; attunement to place and season is deep, and some memories are realities better than anything that can happen again

temperament/inner-life/surrender-to-art.label: Jim's surrender to art and performance
temperament/inner-life/surrender-to-art.line: Surrenders to art completely — wept openly after Camille, tramped through spring rain mourning Marguerite Gauthier as if she had died yesterday, moved by the spirit of 1840 reaching him through an old actress; the Lena dream (her coming barefoot with a reaping-hook at dawn) came out of theater-charged evenings; he wishes the dream were about Ántonia instead

temperament/relational-character.label: Relational and social character
temperament/relational-character.line: Ardent and impulsive in attachment — forms deep bonds with faithful companions and grieves their loss; drawn to the vital and hard-won over the merely advantaged; quick moral judgments that can soften with perspective

work/railway-counsel.label: Railway legal counsel
work/railway-counsel.line: Jim's career: legal counsel for a great Western railway, based in New York but frequently away for weeks at a time

acts-first-reflects-later.text: Acts first in danger, reflects on meaning after — courage is real but context-shaped.

nudges.note: Jim killed the rattlesnake instinctively without running, then later soberly acknowledged the encounter was luck as much as bravery.
Jim reluctantly agreed to sleep at the Cutters' solely because Tony looked so troubled — walked into the danger without full calculation.

ambrosch-broken-saw-lied.text: Ambrosch broke grandfather's saw during the house-building and hid it, then lied about it — Jim knew the truth.

ambrosch-devout.text: Ambrosch sat all morning with his rosary praying silently and aloud, crossing himself — deeply, even slavishly, devout.

ambrosch-fear-purgatory.text: Ambrosch believed his father's soul was in Purgatory for dying by suicide without the Sacrament — it would take years of prayer to free him.

ambrosch-gives-antonia-wages.text: Ambrosch gave Ántonia three hundred dollars — her collected wages from years of hired work — and a set of plated silver when she left for Denver; Mrs. Steavens called it behaving like a man.

ambrosch-head-of-house.text: After Mr. Shimerda's death, Ambrosch became more than ever the head of the Shimerda household — he directed the feelings as well as the fortunes of his womenfolk.

ambrosch-shimerda.text: Ambrosch is one of the Shimerda brothers; he is called 'the crazy boy' — sleeps on a gunny-sack, doesn't wear the shared overcoat even in cold, and showed Jake three prairie dogs he'd shot for food.

ambrosch-shimerda-fat-wife.text: By the time of Jim's visit, Ambrosch Shimerda had a very fat wife who had a farm of her own and bossed her husband.

ambrosch-wanted-antonias-wages.text: Ambrosch planned to pocket every cent of Ántonia's wages himself, providing only such clothing as he thought necessary — Mrs. Harling refused this arrangement.

antonia-age-twenty-four.text: When Jim saw Ántonia after twenty years, she was a stalwart, brown woman, flat-chested, curly hair a little grizzled — battered but not diminished; her eyes were simply Ántonia's eyes, unlike any others he had seen in twenty years.

history.value: At the time of the reunion, Ántonia was barely twenty-four years old despite everything she had endured.

antonia-appearance.text: Ántonia had big warm brown eyes, brown curly wild-looking hair, and glowing dark color in her cheeks; strikingly pretty.

antonia-asks-jim-remember-father.text: Ántonia took Jim's hand and asked him to share what he learned at school, and to never forget her father — Jim promised he never would.

antonia-at-cutters-appearance.text: At the Cutters', Ántonia wore gloves, high-heeled shoes, and feathered bonnets; she copied the dresses of well-off Black Hawk ladies with cheap materials, annoying those ladies.

antonia-at-harlings-character.text: Ántonia's greatest fault at the Harlings was stopping work to play with the children — racing in the orchard and joining hay-fights in the barn.

antonia-baby-portrait.text: Ántonia had her baby's portrait displayed prominently at the Black Hawk photographer's in a large gilt frame — the photographer called it 'Tony Shimerda's baby.'

antonia-belongs-on-farm-not-town.text: Ántonia told Jim she has never had sad spells on the farm as she did in town — she belongs on a farm and is never lonesome there.

antonia-best-dancer.text: Ántonia was declared the best dancer at the Vanni tent — the Vannis themselves said so; she became obsessed with dancing and rushed out at the first call of music.

antonia-birth-alone.text: Ántonia bore her child alone in her room one December evening without calling for help or crying out — her first word was to direct Mrs. Steavens to the fine soap in her trunk.

antonia-bohemian-household.text: At home the Cuzak family speaks Bohemian exclusively — the little ones didn't learn English until school; Ántonia says she has nearly forgotten her own English.

antonia-bohemian-immigrant.text: Ántonia is a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant girl Jim knew from childhood in Nebraska.

antonia-children-number.text: Ántonia has ten or eleven children by the time Jim visits — Anna the eldest daughter, Leo (twelve, born Easter), Rudolph, Yulka, Nina, and others named by Ántonia.

antonia-children-pride-in-her.text: The Cuzak children related to Ántonia the same way the Harling children had — the same pride in her and looking to her for stories and entertainment.

antonia-colic-night-ride.text: Ántonia rode bareback in the night to the Burdens to fetch grandfather when a horse got colic — she threatened to drown herself in the pond if the horse died.

antonia-crushed-by-poverty.text: When grandmother arrived with food, Ántonia came reluctantly to help unpack the hamper, looking crushed in a way Jim had never seen before; she apologized quietly for her mother's crying.

antonia-cuzak-boys-ambrosch-leo-haymow.text: Two of the Cuzak boys — Ambrosch and Leo — slept in the haymow in warm weather; Jim chose to sleep there with them.

antonia-cuzak-boys-well-mannered.text: The older Cuzak boys (Ambrosch, Anton) were straight, well-made fellows with good heads and clear eyes — easy and confidential with Jim as if he were an old family friend.

antonia-cuzak-farm.text: The Cuzak farm is a wide farmhouse with a red barn, ash grove, and cattle-yards, set back on a swell of land near Hastings, Nebraska.

antonia-dances-with-larry-donovan.text: Ántonia went to dances with Larry Donovan, a passenger conductor known as a professional ladies' man.

antonia-dancing-crisis-harlings.text: Ántonia's dancing popularity brought boys to the Harlings' back door and woke Mr. Harling at night — a crisis at the Harling household was building over her dancing.

antonia-dancing-hotel.text: Ántonia was dancing with Lena, Tiny, and Mary Dusak in the hotel dining-room while d'Arnault played — caught out, the girls scattered laughing toward the kitchen.

antonia-dancing-style.text: Ántonia danced with spring and variety — putting in new steps and slides, teaching Jim to dance against and around the beat; dancing with her was always a new adventure.

antonia-departure-denver.text: Ambrosch drove Ántonia and her three trunks to Black Hawk in March for the night train to Denver — he had given her three hundred dollars in collected wages and a set of plated silver.

antonia-destination-black-hawk.text: Ántonia's family was heading to Black Hawk, Nebraska when Jim first heard of her on the train.

antonia-devoted-to-charley-harling.text: Ántonia admired Charley Harling like a prince and was eager to please him — Jim was jealous of her admiration for Charley.

antonia-elderflower-grief.text: The elderflower smell made Ántonia cry — it brought back her father's green bench and his friend who played trombone; she told Jim her feet still remember every path in her old country.

antonia-engaged-larry-donovan.text: Larry Donovan never married Ántonia — he deserted her; she returned home with a baby and settled into being Ambrosch's drudge on the farm.

history.value: Ántonia was engaged to Larry Donovan — she talked about him as if he were president of the railroad; Lena said she was 'sort of innocent' and would always believe him despite others' doubts; Jim said he didn't like Larry and never would.

antonia-english-learner.text: Ántonia refused grandmother's invitation to return to school, saying she had no time to learn — she could work like a man and intended to help make the land a good farm.

history.value: Ántonia was eager to learn English; Jim was one of her first teachers.

antonia-farewell-waving-apron.text: When Jim reached the bottom of the hill and glanced back, Ántonia and the children were still at the windmill — she was waving her apron.

antonia-farm-labor-after-return.text: After returning, Ántonia did the work of a man on the farm all spring and summer — ploughing corn, never wearing her pretty dresses, afflicted with toothache, never leaving the farm.

antonia-farm-struggle-first-ten-years.text: The first ten years on the Cuzak farm were a hard struggle — Cuzak knew little about farming and often grew discouraged; Ántonia's strength and field work carried them through.

antonia-father-still-real.text: Ántonia told Jim her father has been dead all these years yet is more real to her than almost anyone else — she talks to him and consults him; the older she grows the better she knows and understands him.

antonia-field-worker.text: By April, just past her fifteenth birthday, Ántonia was ploughing sod all day with the team alongside Ambrosch — tall, strong, arms burned brown, wearing her father's boots and fur cap.

antonia-frances-dance.text: Frances Harling taught the household to dance that winter and said from the first lesson that Ántonia would make the best dancer among them.

antonia-grateful-harling-housekeeping.text: Ántonia said she learned cooking and housekeeping at the Harlings' and credits those lessons with being able to raise her children well.

antonia-grew-older-fast.text: Jim noticed how much older Ántonia had grown in eight months since her father's death — she had come to them as a child and was now a tall strong young girl with hardened arms, neck like a bole of a tree.

antonia-grief-for-father.text: When Jim arrived, Ántonia ran to him and sobbed over her 'lovely papa' — Jim felt her heart breaking as she clung to him.

antonia-grows-apart-from-jim.text: After the winter Ántonia grew apart from Jim — she was in the fields from sunup to sundown, had no time for him, and admired Ambrosch; she thought of Jim only as a little boy.

antonia-harling-bond.text: Jim observed a basic harmony between Ántonia and Mrs. Harling — both strong, independent natures who loved children, animals, music, rough play, and hearty joviality; Jim couldn't imagine Ántonia anywhere else in Black Hawk.

antonia-harvest-at-burdens.text: During July harvest Ántonia came to work at the Burdens' kitchen; she was gay and responsive and grandmother was in high spirits.

antonia-house-refuge.text: The Steavens house (formerly the Burden house) had always been a refuge to Ántonia — she whispered 'Goodbye, dear house' when she left for Denver.

antonia-images-in-memory-fixed.text: Lying in the haymow Jim reflected that Ántonia had always left images in his mind that did not fade but grew stronger with time — a succession of fixed pictures: the rattlesnake triumph, her father's graveside in snowstorm, her coming in with the work-team at evening.

antonia-inner-fire-unchanged.text: Jim observed that Ántonia had lost teeth and hardened in body, but had kept the fire of life — her inner glow had not faded as it had in so many women who had kept everything else.

antonia-jim-bond-shared-dread.text: Jim and Ántonia sat through Pavel's dying vigil together; she held his hand under the table as the horror unfolded — the experience deepened their bond through shared dread.

antonia-jim-moment-cutters.text: Walking home from the Cutters', Jim felt his full pride and love for Ántonia — she was still his Ántonia, warm and true-hearted; he walked home with his head high.

antonia-learns-english-quickly.text: Ántonia learned English so quickly that by the time school began she could speak as well as any of the Black Hawk children.

antonia-leaves-cutters.text: Ántonia was working as housekeeper at Mrs. Gardener's hotel in Black Hawk — Mrs. Gardener had great confidence in her.

history.value: After the Cutter assault incident Ántonia was frightened and went home to the Shimerdas' farm to stay for a while.

antonia-leaves-harlings-for-cutters.text: Ántonia chose to leave the Harling household rather than give up dancing — she moved to the Cutters' to work for four dollars a week; Mrs. Harling warned her never to come back.

antonia-like-little-girl-again.text: Under the elderflowers at the river, with grief and memory bringing back her father, Ántonia seemed to Jim exactly like the little girl who used to come to the Burden house with Mr. Shimerda.

antonia-liked-jim-more-after-snake.text: After Jim killed the rattlesnake, Ántonia liked him better and never again took a supercilious air with him.

antonia-loves-leo-most.text: Ántonia whispered to Jim that Leo is the worst of all — and she loves him best; she thinks it may be because he came on Easter Day.

antonia-married-cuzak.text: Ántonia married a young Bohemian named Cuzak — a cousin of Anton Jelinek — very soon after Jim's last visit; they were poor and had a large family.

antonia-martha-eldest-married.text: Martha, Ántonia's eldest daughter (the one born before the marriage), is now married and has a baby of her own.

antonia-maternity-aversion-killing.text: Since having children, Ántonia cannot bear to kill anything — even wringing a goose's neck makes her faint.

antonia-natural-born-mother.text: Mrs. Steavens said Ántonia is a natural-born mother — she loved the baby from the first as dearly as if she'd had a ring on her finger and was never ashamed of it.

antonia-never-believed-harm-loved.text: Ántonia told Jim her trouble was she never could believe harm of anybody she loved.

antonia-nina-named-harling.text: Ántonia named one of her daughters Nina after Nina Harling; she said she loved the Burden and Harling children almost as much as her own.

antonia-older-than-jim.text: Ántonia was four years older than Jim.

antonia-only-talks-prices-strength.text: After the winter Ántonia talked of nothing but prices of things and how much she could lift and endure — Jim felt she was too proud of her strength.

antonia-orchard-planted.text: Ántonia and her husband planted every tree in the orchard and carried water to them after full days in the fields — she says she loves them as if they were people; Cuzak knows grafting from working Florida orange groves.

antonia-patience-donovan-excuse.text: Ántonia told Mrs. Steavens she hadn't insisted on a civil marriage because her patience was worn out from waiting — she thought if he saw how well she could do for him, he'd want to stay.

antonia-photos-jim-chicago-kept.text: Ántonia had cut out a photograph of Jim from a Chicago newspaper and kept it; Leo recognized Jim when he drove up to the windmill.

antonia-placed-with-harlings.text: Grandmother saved Ántonia from husking corn all winter by getting her a place to work with the Harlings in Black Hawk.

antonia-predicts-jim-doctor.text: Ántonia told Jim she had set her heart on him becoming a doctor — said he was good with sick people and that her papa always called him an awful smart boy.

antonia-raise-daughter-better.text: Ántonia declared her purpose: to see that her little girl has a better chance than she ever had — that is what she was put in the world for.

antonia-reconciled-harlings.text: Ántonia made up with the Harlings — little Nina was so fond of her that Mrs. Harling overlooked past difficulties; the Harlings' influence with the railroad also kept Larry Donovan in check.

antonia-resilient-dignity.text: Meets catastrophe with quiet dignity — works harder, asks for no pity, refuses to be humbled before others

nudges.note: Ántonia returned from Denver unmarried and pregnant, stood at the wash-tubs, showed calm to Mrs. Steavens, ploughed all summer; Mrs. Steavens marvelled at her calm

antonia-return-disgrace.text: Ántonia returned unmarried and pregnant from Denver — quiet, mournful, refusing sympathy, telling Mrs. Steavens she was 'not married and ought to be'; she showed remarkable calm and dignity throughout.

antonia-rich-mine-of-life.text: Jim, meditating on Ántonia at midnight, felt she was a rich mine of life, like the founders of early races — still with the power to stop one's breath by a gesture that revealed the meaning in common things.

antonia-rooted-in-land.text: Ántonia is rooted in the land — farming life gives her peace and purpose that town life never could

nudges.note: She explicitly told Jim she belongs on a farm, never has sad spells there, and never gets lonesome as she did in town.

antonia-shamed-quarrel-jake.text: Ántonia told the children she was ashamed that she had quarreled with Jake Marpole — she had been saucy and impertinent to him and wished she had behaved better.

antonia-storyteller-voice.text: Ántonia was a gifted storyteller — her voice deep and husky with breath vibrating behind it; everything she said seemed to come right from her heart.

antonia-threshing-story.text: Ántonia drove a grain-wagon during threshing at the Iversons' and witnessed a tramp jump into the threshing machine — she screamed, men stopped the horses, but he was killed.

antonia-trousseau-preparation.text: Ántonia prepared her trousseau at the Steavens house all summer before leaving — hemstitching tablecloths and pillow-cases, buying silver spoons and forks, receiving gifts from the Harlings and from Lena; she worked harder than any girl Mrs. Steavens had ever seen.

antonia-uneasy-about-lena.text: Ántonia was awkward with Lena's visit to the Harlings, worried Mrs. Harling would disapprove given Lena's reputation in the settlement.

antonia-vitality-endures.text: Keeps the fire of life however much the outer body costs — hardship does not drain the inner glow

nudges.note: Jim reflected that Ántonia had lost teeth and grown brown and hardened, but had not lost the fire of life that so many women with easier lives had let fade

antonia-wages-harlings.text: Ántonia was hired by the Harlings at three dollars a week plus shoes; Mrs. Harling kept fifty dollars a year for Ántonia's own use against Ambrosch's objection.

antonia-wants-live-die-here.text: Ántonia told Jim she would be miserable in a city — she wants to live and die where she knows every stack and tree and where all the ground is friendly.

antonia-warns-jim-about-lena.text: Ántonia warned Jim to stay away from Lena Lingard, calling her 'soft that way — she can't help it'; she threatened to tell grandmother if he kept hanging around Lena.

attachment-to-loyal-companions.text: Forms deep, lasting attachments to faithful companions and grieves their loss keenly

nudges.note: Jim's tribute to Jake and Otto — 'things that cannot be bought in any market' — and the unresolved sorrow of never hearing from them again
Jim describes having Ántonia near again as 'how good it was' — her return to daily life fills a gap; and he feels jealousy at her admiration for Charley

attunement-to-place-and-season.text: Intensely attuned to the emotional texture of place and season — reads landscape as moral truth

nudges.note: Jim's extended meditation on Black Hawk winter: the cold sunset as 'the light of truth itself,' summer's greenery as lies, the church window as solace — landscape carries philosophical weight for him
Jim's rendering of late-winter Black Hawk as 'stale and shabby, old and sullen' — the town shrinks to bare stalk; winter is not background but inner weather
A face reminds Jim of Virginia childhood — place-memory lodged deep, surfacing through sensory cue

black-hawk-north-pastures.text: North of Black Hawk, Jim found rough unploughed pastures where the long red grass of early times still grew shaggy over the draws and hillocks — out there he felt at home again.

black-hawk-old-friends-gone.text: When Jim returned to Black Hawk on this visit, most of his old friends were dead or had moved away; the Harlings' yard had strangers in it, the mountain ash was cut down, only a stump of the Lombardy poplar remained.

black-hawk-town-girls-contrast.text: The Black Hawk merchant-class girls were indoorsy and physically inert — believed themselves 'refined' and looked down on the hired country girls who 'worked out.'

blind-darnault-concert.text: Blind d'Arnault was a mulatto pianist from a Louisiana plantation — born blind, self-taught by creeping to Miss Nellie's piano as a child; he played barbarously and wonderfully, his body in constant rocking motion.

burden-farm-only-wooden-house.text: The Burden farm had the only wooden house west of Black Hawk until the Norwegian settlement; neighbors lived in sod houses and dugouts.

burden-homestead-rented-steavens.text: The Burden homestead was rented to 'the Widow Steavens' and her bachelor brother when the family moved to Black Hawk.

cleric-death.text: Gaston Cleric died of pneumonia the winter before Jim's reunion with Ántonia.

cleric-harvard-appointment.text: Cleric accepted an instructorship at Harvard before June and invited Jim to follow him there.

cleric-warns-jim-lena.text: Cleric confronted Jim about Lena, calling her 'perfectly irresponsible,' and told him he would never settle down while playing with the handsome Norwegian.

colonel-raleigh-lena.text: Old Colonel Raleigh — Lena's landlord, a Kentucky widower who had lost his fortune in Lincoln real estate — was charmed by Lena's good looks and gentle manners; he painted and papered her rooms and put in a porcelain bathtub; he and Jim went buggy-riding together talking about Lena and the 'great beauties' of his youth.

coronado-sword-harling-office.text: A Spanish sword and metal stirrup — relics possibly linked to Coronado's expedition — were found by a farmer north of Black Hawk and displayed in the Harling office all one summer; Father Kelly identified the Spanish maker and an abbreviation for the city of Cordova.

crazy-mary-threatens-lena.text: Crazy Mary (Ole Benson's wife) chased Lena across the prairie more than once, threatening to cut her with a corn-knife; Lena hid in Ántonia's feather-bed at the Shimerdas'.

cutter-assault-on-jim.text: Wick Cutter, having planted his silver under Ántonia's bed to lure her to stay alone, returned in the night and attacked Jim — who had taken her place — choking and beating him before Jim fought free and escaped.

cutter-motivation-inheritance.text: Cutter killed his wife out of spite — to prevent her relatives from inheriting; a new state law would have secured the surviving wife one third of the estate, which tormented him.

cutter-murder-suicide.text: Two years before Jim's visit, Wick Cutter bought a pistol, practised target shooting, then shot Mrs. Cutter through the heart while she napped; he shot himself at six o'clock but survived long enough to call in witnesses, declare he had outlived his wife, and dictate that any will she might have made was invalid — his estate was about a hundred thousand dollars.

cutter-old-age-shrivelled.text: In old age Cutter shrivelled until he looked like a little old yellow monkey — his beard and fringe of hair never changed colour; Mrs. Cutter grew a shaking palsy, constantly nodding.

cutter-trick-wife-kansas-city.text: Cutter tricked his wife onto a Kansas City express at Waymore Junction — buying her a ticket to that city, settling her in her seat, then slipping back to Black Hawk on the connecting train — to get home alone.

cuzak-backstory-full.text: Cuzak's father was a shoemaker, his uncle a furrier; he worked as a journeyman furrier in Vienna, spent every evening's wages, came to New York, was blacklisted for working during a strike, went to Florida to grow oranges (hard frost killed his grove and he got malaria), then came to Nebraska to visit Anton Jelinek — saw Ántonia and married her at once, borrowing money from Jelinek for the ring.

cuzak-boys-future-friendship-planned.text: As Jim wandered the rough pastures, his mind was full of pleasant things — trips planned with the Cuzak boys to the Bad Lands and up the Stinking Water; even after the boys grew up there would always be Cuzak himself to tramp a few miles of lighted streets with.

cuzak-character.text: Lena described Cuzak as not a hustler — not a man of much force — but said a rough man would never have suited Tony.

cuzak-farm-paid-worth-five-times.text: Cuzak told Jim the farm is now clear of debt — bought at twenty dollars an acre, now offered a hundred; they also bought a second quarter ten years ago, nearly paid for.

cuzak-jim-hunting-plan.text: Jim invited Ambrosch and Rudolph Cuzak to go hunting with him up on the Niobrara the following summer — Cuzak senior agreed to let the boys off after harvest.

cuzak-longs-for-europe-again.text: Cuzak confessed to Jim that he sometimes nearly runs away when he reads news from the old country; he had never imagined himself becoming a settled farming man.

cuzak-maria-vasak-interest.text: Cuzak was keenly interested in the singer Maria Vasak — she came from his part of Prague and his father mended her shoes when she was a student; he asked Jim about her feet, popularity, and whether she had saved her money.

cuzak-marriage-dynamic.text: Cuzak told Jim Ántonia is a good wife for a poor man — not always strict with him; when he drinks a little too much beer in town she says nothing and asks no questions; they always get along as they did at first.
