cuzak-twenty-six-years-away.text: Cuzak remarked to Jim that it doesn't seem like he has been away from Vienna for twenty-six years.

danish-laundry-girls.text: Four Danish laundry girls lived with Mr. Jensen the laundryman — kind, simple, happy; prettiest not at the dances but at the ironing boards, with bare white arms and rose-flushed cheeks; they danced with rosemary-scented clothes.

darnault-gifts-from-russian-noble.text: d'Arnault owned a gold watch that struck the hours and a topaz ring given by a Russian nobleman who had heard him play in New Orleans.

darnault-happiest-face-virginia.text: d'Arnault's face was the happiest Jim had seen since he left Virginia — the sight stirred a childhood-deep recognition in him.

donovan-deserted-full-account.text: Donovan had been fired and blacklisted for knocking down fares before Ántonia arrived; he was sick when she got there, lived off her money, never hunted real work, then vanished — likely to Mexico where conductors extort half-fares from natives.

drawn-to-crisis-and-drama.text: looks forward to new crises with delight rather than dread

nudges.note: Jim admitted he looked forward to any new crisis with delight when excited voices woke him the morning of Mr. Shimerda's death.

drawn-to-vital-outsiders.text: Drawn to people who grew up hard and carry life-knowledge rather than formal advantages — finds them more real and more interesting

nudges.note: Jim's extended reflection that the hired girls were superior in education and vitality to the 'advantaged' townspeople
Jim's extended contempt for the town boys who looked down on the hired girls, and his satisfaction that those girls eventually became the 'mistresses of rich farms'

draws-meaning-from-place.text: invests particular places with deep personal meaning — returns to them imaginatively even decades later

nudges.note: Jim says Shimerda's grave became the spot most dear to him in all that country; he never passed it without emotion, and he loved the dim superstition behind its placement.
Jim's sudden awareness that he will be homesick for the Black Hawk river after leaving — feeling the sandbars as a world he owns imaginatively

draws-toward-darkness.text: Drawn toward harrowing or extreme experience — does not flinch from witnessing suffering or terror.

nudges.note: Jim volunteered eagerly to stay up all night at a dying man's bedside, and was riveted by Pavel's terrifying wolf confession rather than frightened away.
Jim and Ántonia kept the wolf-wedding story as a private, treasured secret — 'a painful and peculiar pleasure' — rather than finding it merely disturbing.

frances-harling-business-ability.text: Frances Harling was her father's chief clerk, virtually managed the Black Hawk office, and grandfather said she was as good a judge of credits as any banker in the county.

frances-harling-legend-cuzak-family.text: Frances Harling had come down as a heroine in the Cuzak family legend — the Cuzak girls murmured admiringly over her photograph in riding costume.

frances-harling-married.text: Frances Harling was married by the time Jim returned from Harvard; she and her husband managed the Harling interests in Black Hawk.

frances-harling-wick-cutter.text: Frances and grandfather more than once put their wits together to rescue farmers from Wick Cutter's clutches.

frances-reads-jim.text: Frances Harling told Jim that he puts a kind of glamour over the country girls, and that his trouble is that he is romantic — but that Mrs. Harling would come around once he passed his college examinations.

gaston-cleric-character.text: Gaston Cleric was parsimonious about small expenditures, brilliant in personal talk — nearly missed being a great poet by squandering his gift in conversation; in crowds silent, in a small room capable of flashing the exact image from his brain into lamplight.

gaston-cleric-health.text: Cleric came west on physician's advice after a long illness in Italy — he had caught fever at Paestum staying the night among sea temples, fell ill in Naples, and was still doing penance for it when he arrived in Lincoln.

grandfather-character.text: Grandfather was deliberate and personally dignified, not demonstrative, with striking white hair and beard and bright blue eyes.

grandfather-deacon-black-hawk.text: In Black Hawk grandfather became a deacon in the new Baptist Church.

grandfather-faith.text: Grandfather led household prayers each evening, reading Psalms with a sympathetic and compelling voice.

grandfather-graveside-prayer.text: At Mr. Shimerda's grave grandfather prayed without judging — 'no man among us knows what the sleeper knows' — and asked God to be merciful and to incline men's hearts to deal justly with the widow.

grandfather-reconciles-shimerdas.text: Grandfather brought about the reconciliation with the Shimerdas — he engaged Ambrosch and Ántonia for the harvest and forgave the cow debt; he never joined in Jake and Jim's feud.

grandfather-ten-years-nebraska.text: Grandfather had lived in Nebraska for ten years at the time of the great blizzard.

grandfather-vision-cornfields.text: Grandfather had the clear meditative eye to foresee the Nebraska cornfields enlarging until they became the world's cornfields — one of the great economic facts of peace or war.

grandmother-age-arrival.text: Grandmother Burden was fifty-five years old when Jim arrived at the farm.

grandmother-character.text: Grandmother was tall, spare, quick-footed, energetic, with a shrill anxious voice and lively intelligence.

grandmother-charity-shimerdas.text: Grandmother drove to the Shimerdas with a hamper of food — a rooster, potatoes, and provisions — to relieve their winter destitution.

grandmother-indignant-graveyard.text: Grandmother was indignant at the Norwegian church's refusal and vowed to get grandfather to start a more liberal American graveyard in spring.

grandmother-winter-cooking.text: Grandmother kept the household warm, well-fed, and cheerful through the Nebraska winter — ham, bacon, sausage, pies, cakes, and Jim's favourite currant pudding boiled in a bag.

harling-household-dynamics.text: When Mr. Harling was home the house was quiet and children went early to bed; he was autocratic and imperial, demanding all his wife's attention.

harlings-norwegian-neighbors.text: The Harlings were Norwegian neighbors in Black Hawk — Mrs. Harling born in Christiania, Mr. Harling a grain merchant and cattle-buyer from Minnesota.

harry-paine-incident.text: Harry Paine forced a kiss on Ántonia on the Harlings' back porch the Saturday before his wedding; she slapped him and he fled over the fence — Mr. Harling saw it all.

hired-girls-economic-role.text: Bohemian and Scandinavian girls went into service in Black Hawk because they could not get teaching positions — and sent hard-earned dollars home to help clear farm debt; their families became the first to prosper.

hired-girls-social-tension.text: The country hired girls in Black Hawk were a distinct social class — young men of the Progressive Euchre Club risked reputations for a waltz with them, while the girls had come to town to earn and support families.

imaginative-inner-life.text: tends to inhabit an interior imaginative life — daydreaming, mythologizing, feeling kinship with the dead or absent

nudges.note: Jim spent the afternoon alone imagining Mr. Shimerda's spirit resting in the kitchen, and felt as if living among the old man's memories of Bohemia.

jake-character.text: Jake was duller than Otto — barely literate, with a violent temper that tore him apart — but soft-hearted, jovial, hard-working, and too easily imposed upon.

jake-fight-ambrosch.text: Jake knocked Ambrosch down with a blow to the head after Ambrosch ruined a borrowed horse-collar and then kicked at Jake; Ambrosch was stunned with a nosebleed.

jake-otto-departed-west.text: Jake and Otto left Nebraska on the westbound train after helping the Burdens move to Black Hawk — Jim never saw them again.

jake-otto-yankee-girl-mine.text: Jake and Otto were last heard from at the Yankee Girl Mine in Colorado; Jim's follow-up letter came back unclaimed.

jelinek-homestead-near-black-hawk.text: Anton Jelinek had taken a homestead near Black Hawk and was learning English at the school by the mill along with the little children.

jelinek-saloon-black-hawk.text: Jelinek rented out his homestead, moved to Black Hawk, and ran a saloon where Bohemian and German farmers could eat lunch, drink beer, and speak their own languages; he asked Jim to stop coming out of respect for grandfather.

jelinek-war-faith.text: As a boy Jelinek served as altar boy to a priest during the Prussian war, carrying the Sacrament among cholera soldiers; he believes that faith preserved him from sickness — he saw too much to doubt prayer for the dead.

jim-admires-hired-girls.text: Jim felt these immigrant country girls — who had grown up hard and learned from poverty and life — were more interesting and better educated than the townspeople who had 'advantages.'

jim-age-nineteen-boston.text: Jim was nineteen years old when he left Lincoln and joined Cleric in Boston.

jim-age-over-forty.text: Jim is over forty years old.

jim-antonia-as-anchor.text: Carries Ántonia's image as the deepest anchor of his interior life — she is part of his mind regardless of distance

nudges.note: Jim told Ántonia her idea is part of his mind and influences hundreds of choices; he means to carry her face always — the closest, realest face at the bottom of his memory

jim-antonia-fairest.text: Jim privately thought Ántonia was still 'fairest of them all' — like Snow-White — as she and the other girls walked downtown in their finery.

jim-antonia-friendship-coldness.text: After the fight, a distinct coldness opened between the Burdens and the Shimerdas; Ántonia jeered at Jake for weeks; Jim hotly declared he would never be friends with the Shimerdas again.

jim-antonia-parting-declaration.text: Jim told Ántonia he thinks of her more often than anyone else in that part of the world — she is part of his mind, influences all his tastes, and is the closest realest face at the very bottom of his memory.

jim-beaten-cutter-shame.text: After being beaten by Cutter, Jim was humiliated and furious — he refused a doctor and begged grandmother to keep everyone away, including Ántonia, fearing the story's exposure; he briefly hated Ántonia for having put him in the position.

jim-bitter-antonia-pity.text: Seeing Ántonia's baby portrait, Jim felt he must see her again — he could forgive her anything except throwing herself away on a cheap man like Donovan.

history.value: Jim was bitterly disappointed in Ántonia for becoming an object of pity and could not forgive her for it — he tried to shut her out of his mind.

jim-black-hawk-restlessness.text: Jim felt moody, restless, and caged in Black Hawk as a senior — still marching to school bells while Charley Harling was at Annapolis; he prowled the cold streets at night scowling at the small sleeping houses.

jim-black-hawk-winter.text: Jim experienced the bleakness of prairie-town winters in Black Hawk — cold streets, the hunger for colour, the glowing church window the only warmth on a dark walk home.

jim-capacity-for-disappointment.text: High idealization of those he loves makes the fall into disappointment sharp and unforgiving

nudges.note: Jim could not forgive Ántonia for becoming an object of pity — his bitter disappointment blocked compassion

jim-capacity-for-forgiveness.text: Can move from sharp disappointment back to forgiveness when drawn by affection — but bitterness at a perceived betrayal of worth lingers

nudges.note: Jim told himself he could forgive Ántonia if she hadn't thrown herself away on a cheap man — the anger at Donovan replaced the anger at her

jim-childhood-home.text: Jim grew up in a small prairie town in Nebraska.

jim-commencement-speech.text: Jim gave the commencement oration at the Black Hawk Opera House — Mrs. Harling attended and told him afterward she had not believed he could do as well; she gave him a silk umbrella with his name on it.

jim-contempt-black-hawk-life.text: Jim saw Black Hawk's domestic life as a tyranny of evasion and negation — people living like mice, bridling every natural appetite to propitiate the gossip; he hated the furtive repression.

jim-dedicates-speech-shimerda.text: Jim privately dedicated his commencement speech to Mr. Shimerda — he had been thinking of him when he wrote it; he told Ántonia, who burst into tears and embraced him.

jim-drifting-at-university.text: Jim admitted he was drifting in Lincoln — Lena had broken up his serious mood and he was no longer interested in his classes; he played and idled with Lena, Ordinsky, and Colonel Raleigh.

jim-eleventh-birthday.text: Jim's eleventh birthday fell on January 20th.

jim-feared-antonia-aged.text: Jim admitted it was perhaps cowardice that kept him from visiting for twenty years — he dreaded finding Ántonia aged and broken; some memories are realities better than anything that can happen again.

jim-grandparents-nebraska.text: Jim's grandparents live in Nebraska and took him in after his parents died.

jim-harvard-completion.text: Jim completed his academic course at Harvard two years after leaving Lincoln, then went home before law school.

jim-intellectual-awakening.text: Cleric introduced Jim to the world of ideas — the first entry into that world made everything else fade; Jim knew he would never be a scholar because mental excitement always sent him rushing back to the figures of his Nebraska past.

jim-lincoln-room.text: Jim rented two rooms for the price of one from an old couple near the edge of Lincoln — a tiny unheated bedroom (a linen-closet) and a study with a green-topped table facing west over the prairie, a large map of ancient Rome on the wall, and a Pompeii photo Cleric gave him.

jim-mourns-marguerite-rain.text: After Camille, Jim tramped through puddles and lilac-scented spring rain mourning Marguerite Gauthier 'as if she had died only yesterday' — sighing with the spirit of 1840 that had reached him through an infirm old actress across years and languages.

jim-moves-to-black-hawk.text: Jim moved to Black Hawk at age thirteen when his grandparents decided they were too old for heavy farm work.

jim-mythologizes-land.text: Invests landscapes and shared moments with mythic, lasting meaning

nudges.note: The plough-against-the-sun vision struck him as heroic and cosmic — 'a picture writing on the sun' — and the Coronado story amplified the land's legendary weight.
The old road gave Jim an overwhelming sense of coming home to himself — he called the road 'the road of Destiny' and said it determined all they could ever be.

jim-no-children.text: Jim told Ántonia he has no children; she seemed embarrassed for him and jokingly offered him Leo.

jim-not-a-scholar.text: Cannot lose himself in impersonal things for long — mental excitement always returns him to the specific people and places of his own past

nudges.note: Cleric's intellectual world dazzled him but he knew he would never be a scholar: every quickening of mind sent him rushing back to Jake, Otto, Peter and the Nebraska landscape.

jim-origin-virginia.text: Jim was born in Virginia and lived there until age ten, when his parents died.

jim-patria-revelation.text: Reading Virgil's Georgics, Jim absorbed Cleric's gloss that 'patria' meant not a nation but one's own small rural neighborhood — a thought that reframed his Nebraska past as his own country and source.

jim-plans-university.text: Jim decided to do college-requirement work that summer and enter the university freshman class in the fall — he wanted to get away from Black Hawk as soon as possible.

jim-prizes-vital-lived-in.text: Prizes those who have lived hard and risen by their own effort — finds genuine beauty where others see only roughness

nudges.note: Watching Lena 'so smooth and sunny and well-cared-for' after growing up barefoot with Crazy Mary chasing her, Jim thought it wonderful she had got on; he said she had no one but herself to thank.

jim-protective-of-memory.text: Guards cherished memories against the risk of present disappointment — prefers the image to the encounter when the stakes are high

nudges.note: Jim stayed away from Ántonia for twenty years partly from fear of finding her aged and broken — 'some memories are realities, and are better than anything that can ever happen to one again'

jim-railway-career.text: Jim is legal counsel for one of the great Western railways.

jim-reassures-antonia-father-spirit.text: Jim told Ántonia he had felt her father's presence on the day the family went to view the body — sure he was heading back to Bohemia — and that he still thinks of him as being among the woods and fields he loved.

jim-rejects-purgatory-belief.text: Jim rejected Ambrosch's belief that Mr. Shimerda's soul was in torment — he almost knew it wasn't true — yet the idea of Purgatory came back on him crushingly after he went to bed.

jim-river-farewell-feeling.text: Swimming in the river alone before the girls arrived, Jim realized for the first time he would be homesick for that river after he left — the sandbars and willows were a world he had explored with Charley Harling.

jim-saturday-night-dances.text: Jim never missed a Saturday night dance at the Vanni pavilion — country boys rode in from miles away and all the country girls were on the floor.

jim-self-deceiving-nobility.text: Constructs noble-sounding justifications for self-serving choices — honest enough to recognize the self-deception immediately after

nudges.note: Jim almost convinced himself he was leaving Lincoln for Lena's benefit, to free her to marry; he noted 'it is so necessary to be a little noble!'

jim-sense-coming-home-to-himself.text: On the old road, Jim had the sense of coming home to himself — of having found out what a little circle man's experience is; the feelings of his first night in Nebraska, bedded in straw as a wondering child, were so near he could touch them.

jim-shame-reputation.text: Cares intensely about his reputation and how events will be told — humiliation is almost worse than the physical injury

nudges.note: After the beating Jim's overriding concern was that no one find out; he begged grandmother harder than he had ever begged for anything to keep it quiet.

jim-sneaks-out-dances.text: Jim stopped going to the Firemen's Hall dances after grandmother wept and said it brought blame on the family; he kept his promise and spent spring evenings reading Latin for college entrance.

history.value: Jim secretly climbed out his bedroom window on Saturday nights to attend the Firemen's Hall dances — he changed his shirt and coat, waited for his grandparents to sleep, and soon stopped feeling ashamed.

jim-surrenders-to-art.text: Surrenders to art and performance completely — weeps openly, mourns fictional characters as real losses, carries the emotion out into the world afterward

nudges.note: Jim wept unrestrainedly at Camille's death scene, then tramped through rain mourning Marguerite as if she had died the day before — the feeling was wholly real to him.

jim-surrenders-to-charm.text: Surrenders easily to the company of an enchanting person — lets warmth and ease displace duty without remorse in the moment

nudges.note: Jim admitted he was drifting — Lena had broken up his serious mood entirely and he didn't care about classes; he played and idled all that Lincoln spring without regret.

jim-wife-genevieve.text: Jim's wife is Genevieve Whitney Burden, daughter of a distinguished man; she has her own fortune and lives her own life.

johnnie-gardener-character.text: Johnnie Gardener was an affectionate little man who adored his wife Molly (Mrs. Gardener) and knew he would barely be a hotel clerk without her; her name was on the hotel bus, his ring, and his watch-case.

krajiek-exploits-shimerdas.text: Krajiek overcharged the Shimerdas for a cookstove and sold them worn-out horses at prices for good workteams.

krajiek-suspected-but-cleared.text: The coroner said but for grandfather he might have charged Krajiek; Krajiek acted like a guilty man, but the physical evidence confirmed suicide; he may have felt some remorse for his indifference to Shimerda's misery.

larry-donovan-character.text: Larry Donovan was a passenger conductor — cold and distant with men, familiar and manipulative with women; shared his 'unappreciated worth' as a secret to make foolish hearts ache over him.

lena-appearance-prairie.text: Lena had deep violet eyes with a soft confiding expression, ruddy yellow hair burned by the sun, and arms and legs of miraculous whiteness despite constant exposure.

lena-dancing-style.text: Lena danced indolently, dreamily — violet eyes half-closed, perfume of sachet powder; she danced every dance like a waltz of coming home, fated return; exciting at first, then sultry and restless.

lena-dream-recurring.text: Jim had a recurring dream of Lena Lingard coming to him barefoot across stubble at dawn with a reaping-hook, saying 'now they are all gone, and I can kiss you as much as I like'; he wished he dreamed it about Ántonia instead.

lena-dressmaker-san-francisco.text: Lena moved her dressmaking business to San Francisco at Tiny's urging and has a fine class of trade there.

lena-dressmaker-talent.text: Lena's dressmaking success puzzled Jim — she was easy-going, without push or self-assertiveness, but she had a natural talent for knowing 'what people looked well in'; clients said she had 'style' and overlooked her habitual lateness and budget overruns.

lena-friendship-with-jim.text: After Lena came to Black Hawk, Jim often met her on errands and walked with her; she charmed him with easy talk about dresses and hotel gossip.

lena-hard-childhood-detail.text: Lena described her farm childhood: always three to a bed, always lugging babies, a cross man, work piling up around a sick mother — she never had privacy except when alone with the cattle.

lena-homesick-for-family.text: Despite her determination to be done with farm life, Lena confided to Jim that she got awful homesick for her brothers and sisters.

lena-independence-ambition.text: Lena opened a dressmaking shop in the Raleigh Block on O Street in Lincoln — she had made a 'real good start' and was building a house for her mother that summer.

history.value: Lena declared she intended to move to another town, go into business for herself, and get her mother out of the old sod house — she said the men would never do it.

lena-lapp-ancestry.text: Lena's paternal grandfather married a Lapp woman — his family felt dreadful about it; Lena half-jokingly attributed her own wild streak to that Lapp blood.

lena-lincoln-theater.text: Lena went with Jim to the theater that spring — Joseph Jefferson in 'Rip Van Winkle,' 'Shenandoah,' 'Robin Hood,' and 'Camille'; she was inflexible about paying for her own seat and gave herself over to plays with fatalistic completeness.

lena-lingard-background.text: Lena Lingard grew up herding cattle barefoot and bareheaded in the Norwegian settlement west of Squaw Creek, knitting stockings for her many younger siblings.

lena-lingard-comes-to-town.text: Lena came to Black Hawk to work for Mrs. Thomas the dressmaker, determined to learn sewing, support her mother, and be done with farm life.

lena-no-interest-in-marriage.text: Lena said she did not want to marry Nick Svendsen or any other man — she had seen enough of married life and wanted independence to help her mother.

lena-not-home-six-years.text: By the time of Jim's visit to Ántonia, Lena had not been back to Nebraska for six years.

lena-ordinsky-proposals.text: Ordinsky (the Polish violin teacher) had proposed to Lena multiple times; she accepted the flowers with amusement and refused without rancor.

lena-photo-plump-hat.text: Lena's photograph showed a comely woman, a trifle too plump, in a hat a trifle too large, but with her old lazy eyes and dimpled ingenuousness still at the corners of her mouth.

lena-renunciatory-farewell.text: Lena sent Jim away with a soft, renunciatory kiss and never tried to hold him back — she said 'I oughtn't to have begun it' but owned a little foolishness about him from early on.

lena-speech-candor.text: Lena had picked up all the conventional small-town expressions from Mrs. Thomas's shop, but her use of them — with her caressing intonation and naive delivery — was divinely absurd; she was 'almost as candid as Nature.'

lena-talked-about.text: Lena had been 'talked about' in the Norwegian settlement — accused of making Ole Benson lose his sense; Ántonia was cautious about Mrs. Harling's reception of her.

leo-cuzak-character.text: Leo Cuzak has a faun-like face, gold-green deep-set eyes, tawny fleece of hair down the back of his neck, and a wild restless spirit — always riding unbroken colts and testing danger; he played Mr. Shimerda's old violin by ear.

leo-skeptical-sceptical-like-mrs-shimerd.text: Leo's habitual scepticism reminded Jim of the old Mrs. Shimerda — a direct inheritance in spirit; Leo said of Mr. Harling 'He wasn't any Rockefeller.'

marek-shimerda.text: Marek is one of the Shimerda children — disabled, with webbed fingers, who made animal noises (barking, whinnying); he tried to be agreeable as if making up for his deficiencies.

marek-shimerda-institution.text: Marek Shimerda grew violent and was sent away to an institution before Ántonia's return from Denver.

mary-dusak-appearance.text: Mary Dusak was broad and brown, slightly marked by smallpox but handsome — beautiful chestnut hair in coils, low smooth forehead, commanding dark eyes; bold, resourceful, and unscrupulous.

mr-shimerda-antonia-darling.text: Grandmother said Ántonia was Mr. Shimerda's darling and was like a right hand to him — he left her alone in a hard world.

mr-shimerda-bohemia-forest.text: Mr. Shimerda told stories about playing fiddle at weddings and dances in Bohemia, and about a great forest full of game (belonging to the nobles) where his family used to steal wood on moonlit nights; a white hart lived there.

mr-shimerda-came-against-will.text: Mr. Shimerda never wanted to emigrate; his wife drove the decision for the sake of Ambrosch's future — Shimerda wept leaving the musician friends he loved in Bohemia.

mr-shimerda-cause-homesickness.text: Jim believed it was homesickness that killed Mr. Shimerda — a longing for Bohemia, its forests, music, and friends that Nebraska could never replace.

mr-shimerda-death-suicide.text: Mr. Shimerda shot himself in the barn — he prepared carefully, dressed in clean clothes, kissed his daughters, then lay down in the bunk near the ox stalls and fired with his toe.

mr-shimerda-declining-health.text: Mr. Shimerda's Christmas visit showed him visibly restored by the Burden household's order and comfort — he sat in deep peace, knelt before the Christmas tree, and left blessing both grandmother and Jim.

history.value: Mr. Shimerda was sick much of the time and seemed to live in a torpor; Ántonia was the only one who could rouse him.

mr-shimerda-fiddle.text: In Nebraska Mr. Shimerda stopped playing the violin entirely — at most touching the strings with his fingers; the music died with his separation from Bohemia.

history.value: Mr. Shimerda brought his fiddle with him to Nebraska.

mr-shimerda-marriage-backstory.text: Ántonia revealed her father did not have to marry her mother — she was a poor girl working in his mother's house; he was older and chose to marry her out of kindness rather than pay her off; his brothers quarrelled with him for it and his mother never let Mrs. Shimerda enter her house again.

mr-shimerda-plea-teach-antonia.text: Mr. Shimerda gave grandmother a bilingual alphabet book and begged her to teach Ántonia English — a moment Jim says he will never forget.

mr-shimerda-sadness.text: Mr. Shimerda's smile was full of sadness and pity; Jim never forgot that expression.

mr-shimerda-weaver.text: Mr. Shimerda was a skilled weaver by trade, working on tapestries and upholstery materials in Bohemia.

mrs-cutter-character.text: Mrs. Cutter was a near-giantess — raw-boned, iron-grey haired, hysterical-eyed, face always flushed; horse-toothed; perpetually at war with her husband over inheritance, expenses, and fidelity; Jim saw a gleam of insanity in her eyes.

mrs-gardener-character.text: Mrs. Gardener ran the Boys' Home Hotel — tall, dark, severe, best-dressed woman in Black Hawk; guests felt they were receiving a favour staying there.

mrs-harling-champions-jim-university.text: Mrs. Harling vigorously championed Jim going to college when his grandparents had misgivings — lonely for Charley, she called Jim in to play for him; grandfather had such respect for her that he would not go against her.

mrs-harling-character.text: Mrs. Harling was short, square, and charged with energy — quick to anger and laughter, jolly to her soul, incapable of being negative or perfunctory.

mrs-harling-cool-toward-jim.text: Mrs. Harling came to Jim's commencement and praised his speech; the coolness between them thawed — she gave him a silk umbrella.

history.value: Mrs. Harling was a little cool toward Jim because he continued to champion Ántonia after Ántonia left the Harling household.

mrs-harling-warning-cutters.text: Mrs. Harling told Ántonia that going to work for the Cutters would be her ruin and that she could never come back to the Harling house if she did.

mrs-shimerda-driven-emigration.text: Mrs. Shimerda orchestrated the emigration entirely for Ambrosch's prospects — land, cattle, wealth for her sons and husbands for her daughters; she had no regret about uprooting her husband.

mrs-shimerda-grasping.text: Mrs. Shimerda was conceited, boastful, and grasping — she complained about everything in the Burden house, talked about all grandmother had that she did not, and left with an iron pot she cadged.

mrs-shimerda-milk-cow.text: Grandfather forgave Mrs. Shimerda the remaining fifteen dollars on the cow — the debt was cancelled entirely.

history.value: Mrs. Shimerda paid grandfather ten dollars for a milk cow, with fifteen more due after their first harvest.

nebraska-prairie-transformed.text: When Jim rode out in August he saw the old pastureland broken into wheatfields and cornfields, sod houses replaced by wooden ones — the prairie transformed; he thought it like watching a great man grow.

norwegian-graveyard-refused-shimerda.text: The Norwegian church officers voted to refuse Mr. Shimerda burial in their graveyard; nearest Catholic cemetery was at Black Hawk, weeks away by wagon.

old-figures-rise-at-university.text: Whenever Jim's consciousness was quickened at university, old Nebraska figures — Jake, Otto, Russian Peter — rose vividly in him; they stood out 'strengthened and simplified, like the image of the plough against the sun,' and accompanied him through all new experiences.

old-road-found-in-pasture.text: Walking north of Black Hawk, Jim found a surviving half-mile of the original road that ran to his grandfather's farm and the Shimerdas' — everywhere else ploughed under, this stretch still visible as wheel-ruts washed deep like grizzly's claw-marks.

ordinsky-lena-protector.text: Ordinsky, the Polish violin teacher across the hall, watched over Lena with fierce protectiveness — suspicious of Jim at first, then accepting him as a fellow guardian; quarrelsome and proud, he wrote a furious article attacking Lincoln's musical taste and felt he had Jim's chivalric support.

otto-cabinetmaker-skills.text: Otto Fuchs was apprenticed to a cabinetmaker in the old country and was handy with tools; he built Jim a sleigh from a wooden goods-box and bobs.

otto-coffin-maker.text: Otto Fuchs, as the only cabinetmaker in the neighbourhood, was set to work building Mr. Shimerda's coffin.

otto-drifting-labourer.text: Otto was already one of those drifting, case-hardened labourers who never marry or have children of their own — yet fond of children.

otto-fuchs-background.text: Otto Fuchs is Austrian-born; came to America young and led an adventurous life in mining camps and cow outfits in the Far West.

otto-fuchs-ear.text: Otto Fuchs lost part of his left ear in a Wyoming blizzard when he was a stage-driver.

otto-grey-gelding-ruined.text: The grey gelding grandfather lent Otto for the Black Hawk ride was never the same horse afterward — the long trip through deep snow broke his endurance.

otto-mother-austria.text: Otto's old mother in Austria sent him paper Christmas figures every year; he kept them under the lining of his cowboy trunk.

otto-singer-church.text: Otto Fuchs had a good baritone voice and led the singing at church services held at the sod schoolhouse; on Saturday nights he sang cowboy songs.

pavel-health.text: Pavel died a few days after his confession and was buried in the Norwegian graveyard.

history.value: Pavel was often sick, with a hoarse cough and a gaunt frame.
Pavel, gravely ill and coughing blood, summoned Mr. Shimerda and Ántonia to hear a deathbed confession about a terrible thing he had done in Russia involving wolves at a wedding.

pavel-peter-background.text: Pavel and Peter were Russian settlers, the strangest and most aloof of all the first settlers; Krajiek had cheated them in a trade so they avoided him.

pavel-wolf-wedding-story.text: As young men in Russia, Pavel and Peter were groomsmen at a wedding; a wolf pack attacked the seven-sledge party on the return journey in winter — sledges were overtaken one by one, screaming passengers lost to the wolves, until only the groom's sledge remained.

peter-debt-wick-cutter.text: Peter was unable to meet a note due November 1 and was forced to pay an exorbitant bonus on renewal, giving Wick Cutter mortgages on his pigs, horses, and milk cow; the debt had grown from an original $200 through repeated bonus-laden renewals.

peter-gone-cook.text: After Pavel died, Peter sold everything and left Nebraska to work as a cook in a railway construction camp employing Russians.

plough-against-sun-vision.text: Jim witnessed a plough left on an upland farm silhouetted heroically against the full disk of the setting sun — black against molten red, then vanished as the sun dropped; he called it 'a picture writing on the sun.'

rattlesnake-kill-mock-adventure.text: Jim later reflected that the snake encounter was a lucky mock-adventure: the snake was old and slow, the spade was borrowed by chance, and Ántonia's presence was essential to his feeling brave.

road-of-destiny-declaration.text: Sitting on the old road, Jim felt it had been the road of Destiny for both him and Ántonia — the early accidents of fortune predetermined all they could ever be; whatever they had missed, they possessed together the precious, incommunicable past.

romantic-ardent.text: Naturally romantic and ardent in disposition, meets people and enterprises with impulsiveness

nudges.note: Friend describes Jim's disposition as romantic and ardent; disappointments have not chilled it; still meets new things with boyhood impulsiveness at over forty

At age ten, crossing into unknown Nebraska prairie at night, Jim felt not homesickness but awe and wonder — erased between earth and sky — a sensibility open to vastness rather than retreating from it
As a ten-year-old Jim sat alone in the garden and felt completely dissolved into the prairie, experiencing pure happiness — an early signal of his deep attunement to landscape and feeling
Jim remembers that first Nebraska autumn as glorious; rode freely across unfenced prairie trusting the pony; sunflower roads became to him permanently the roads to freedom

Jim describes all those fall afternoons with Ántonia on the prairie as never-the-same-but-never-gotten-used-to; the late afternoon light a triumphant lifting-up of day — he is deeply attuned to beauty and carries it lifelong
Frances Harling's diagnosis that Jim puts a 'kind of glamour' over the country girls and that his trouble is that he is romantic — affirmed rather than denied by Jim

rudolph-cuzak-character.text: Rudolph Cuzak is six foot two with a chest like a young blacksmith and a deep baritone voice — the eldest son at home; he told the Cutter murder story at supper.

russians-bad-luck-feared.text: The Russians had such persistent bad luck that neighbors feared them and tried to put them out of mind.

self-deprecating-honesty.text: Honest about the gap between how events are narrated and how they actually unfolded — resists inflated self-myth.

nudges.note: Jim explicitly recalled the snake adventure as a 'mock adventure' with the game 'fixed by chance,' undermining the heroic gloss Ántonia put on it.

shimerda-ambrosch-farming-decisions.text: Ambrosch proved far-seeing: he sold the oxen to a German settler and bought horses; he worked Marek hard but could never teach him to cultivate corn.

shimerda-buried-crossroads.text: Mr. Shimerda was buried at the southwest corner stake of the Shimerda land — Mrs. Shimerda's insistence — where two roads would eventually cross, suggesting an old Bohemian crossroads custom for suicides.

shimerda-family-nearest-neighbors.text: The Shimerda family (Ántonia's family) were the Burdens' nearest neighbors in Nebraska.

shimerda-girls-sleep-hole.text: Yulka and Ántonia slept in a small round hole scooped into the earth wall of the cave, on straw with quilts — Mr. Shimerda showed grandmother in despair.

shimerda-grave-beloved-spot.text: Mr. Shimerda's grave became the spot most dear to Jim in all that country — roads curved around it in later years, the tall red grass never mowed, like a little island; Jim never passed without emotion.

shimerda-homestead-krajiek.text: The Shimerdas bought their Nebraska homestead from Peter Krajiek at an inflated price arranged before they left Bohemia.

shimerda-savings-lost.text: Mr. Shimerda left Bohemia with over a thousand dollars after passage money; exchange losses in New York and Krajiek's prices for land, horses, oxen, and machinery left them nearly destitute; he still had some savings but barely enough to survive the winter.

shimerda-settlement-wild-place.text: By mid-winter the Shimerdas were reduced to near-starvation: rotten frozen potatoes begged from the post-office discard, almost no flour, no coffee, feet wrapped in rags, sharing one overcoat among the whole family.

history.value: The Shimerdas settled on a wild place with no garden, no chicken-house, and very little broken land.

shimerda-spring-plan.text: By spring the Shimerdas had a new log house built in March with neighbours' help, a windmill on credit, a chicken-house, poultry, and a milk cow — fairly equipped to begin farming.

history.value: Mr. Shimerda planned to buy a cow and chickens, plant a garden, and build a new house in spring — he and Ambrosch had already split logs for the house but they were buried in snow.

snap-judgments-on-people.text: Forms sharp moral judgments quickly but can moderate them when perspective arrives.

nudges.note: Jim was furious at Mrs. Shimerda and felt coldness spill toward Ántonia; grandmother's gentle reframe ('poverty brings out grasping') shifted his view.
Jim hotly declared he believed all the Shimerdas were 'like Krajiek and Ambrosch underneath' immediately after the fight — then later moderated this.

sun-moon-farewell-vision.text: Walking homeward with Ántonia at sunset, Jim saw the sun and moon face each other on opposite edges of the level land — every stalk and furrow standing sharp; he felt the old pull of the earth and wished he could be a little boy again.

sylvester-lovett-lena.text: Sylvester Lovett, the banker's-son cashier, fell daft over Lena Lingard at the dances — took all her dances, drove to visit her, then fled into a marriage with an older widow to escape; Jim felt contempt for him.

three-marys-settled-families.text: By the time of Jim's visit, the three Bohemian Marys had settled down with large families; Mary Svoboda is considered the best butter-maker in the country and a fine manager.

three-marys-stories.text: The 'three Bohemian Marys' — Mary Dusak, Mary Svoboda, and another — were heroines of scandalous stories; considered dangerous but such good cooks they never lacked a place.

tiny-lena-san-francisco.text: Tiny persuaded Lena Lingard to relocate her dressmaking business from Lincoln to San Francisco, where Lena has a fine class of trade.

tiny-lost-toes.text: Tiny lost three toes to frostbite in the Klondike — she mentioned it casually with no apparent sensitivity.

tiny-most-adventurous-life.text: Jim observed that of all the Black Hawk girls and boys, Tiny Soderball was to lead the most adventurous life and achieve the most solid worldly success.

tiny-san-francisco.text: Tiny returned from the Klondike with a considerable fortune and settled in San Francisco.

tiny-soderball-appearance.text: Tiny Soderball was trim and slender with lively little feet and pretty ankles — quicker in speech and lighter in movement than the other girls.

tiny-soderball-family-farm.text: Tiny Soderball's family had put in twenty acres of rye on their farm; her mother's homesickness eased once they had rye flour from the mill.

tiny-soderball-introduced.text: Tiny Soderball is a hired girl from the country who came to work at the Boys' Home Hotel in Black Hawk; she and Lena were friends.

tiny-soderball-seattle.text: Tiny Soderball went to Alaska, endured the Chilkoot Pass and Yukon flatboats, helped found Dawson City, ran a log hotel, inherited Johnson's Hunker Creek gold claim, and accumulated a considerable fortune over nearly ten years in the Klondike.

history.value: Tiny Soderball went West to Seattle with definite plans and is now running a sailors' lodging-house in a waterfront building offered by a promoter from Mrs. Gardener's hotel.

tiny-worn-out-interest.text: Jim saw Tiny in Salt Lake City in 1908: satisfied but not elated — she seemed to have lost the faculty of becoming interested in anything except making money.

twenty-years-passed-antonia.text: Twenty years passed between Jim's farewell to Ántonia and his visit to the Cuzak farm — business took him West often but he always deferred the stop.

vanni-dancing-pavilion.text: The Vannis set up a dancing pavilion tent near the Danish laundry on a vacant lot in Black Hawk — Mrs. Vanni taught children, Mr. Vanni (harpist) taught older ones; open until ten, closing to 'Home, Sweet Home.'

western-passion.text: Loves the West with personal passion and invests deeply in its people and future

nudges.note: Jim loves his railway country with personal passion; raises capital for Wyoming and Montana enterprises; helps young men in mines, timber, oil
Jim's searing contempt for Black Hawk's gossip-driven, repressed domestic life suggests the West's people could also disappoint him

wick-cutter-appearance.text: Cutter had a pink bald head, soft glistening yellow whiskers he brushed nightly like a woman, factory-white teeth, and red rough skin; he wore yellow gloves and a check cap when driving his trotting horse.

wick-cutter-character.text: Wick Cutter was an inveterate gambler, notoriously dissolute with women, hypocritically pious — quoted Poor Richard, contributed to churches 'for sentiment,' but had corrupted two Swedish servant girls; Jim detested his pink bald head and glistening yellow whiskers.

wick-cutter-introduced.text: Wick Cutter is the Black Hawk money-lender who trapped Peter in compounding debt; he is described as merciless and of evil name throughout the county.

widow-steavens-meets-jim.text: The Widow Steavens, tenant of Jim's grandfather's farm, agreed to tell Jim everything about Ántonia's failed marriage and the baby.

wolf-story-jim-antonia-secret.text: The wolf-wedding story became a private secret between Jim and Ántonia — they kept it from everyone else and it haunted Jim's imagination at night.

yulka-shimerda.text: Yulka is Ántonia's younger sister; she rode with Jim and Ántonia on the first sleigh-ride and begged to stay out on the open prairie.
